title: Beneath the surface
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE IMF’s staff-level agreement with Pakistan on the fourth balance-of-payments and the third climate financing reviews came with little drama — which itself says something.
The mission spent two weeks in Islamabad, wrapped up the 2026 Article IV consultation, and left with a deal that releases $1.2bn once the IMF Executive Board approves it. Nobody expected a different outcome. The Fund is unlikely to push hard against a borrower that is hitting its fiscal targets. Compare this with March, when talks went virtual, ended without an agreement, and dragged on until the Board cleared funds in May. The recent round made fewer headlines because the hard bargaining over the budget had already been done. The current budget is built around a primary surplus of 2pc of GDP, and the lender is now collecting on that commitment. A programme that has settled into a routine reassures markets. It also shows how little room Islamabad has to depart from the script.
The lender’s own assessment is generous. It says the authorities have successfully navigated the fallout of the Middle East conflict and that policies have preserved stability. Reserves stand at about $21.5bn and inflation has eased from its May peak. Yet, a closer look shows that, at 10.3pc in September, inflation remains well above the State Bank’s medium-term target range. Last year’s growth of 3.6pc, with an annual population growth of nearly 2pc, leaves per capita gains thin.
The World Bank put poverty at about 42.4pc for 2025, and said growth was too weak to prevent an additional 1.9m people from slipping below the line in a single year. Exports tell the same story. Goods exports fell about 6pc to $30.1bn, of which textiles accounted for $17.9bn. Imports rose 8pc to $69.8bn, widening the merchandise trade deficit to $39.6bn. Growth in IT services kept total exports near $40bn, which though welcome, is no substitute for a manufacturing base that sells more abroad.
The recommendations deserve more attention than the headline figure. The lender wants the fuel support scheme phased out, calling it costly and too broadly targeted. Unwinding a broad subsidy is politically harder than agreeing to end it on paper. It also wants timely tariff adjustments so that the circular debt does not return, a medium-term tax strategy, private participation in power distribution, better governance of SOEs, and progress on privatisation. Many who have read the earlier review statements will recognise the list. When the same agenda is repeated, the question one must ask is: how much has changed? The Fund’s language of commitment does not answer it. The tranche will arrive. What the government has yet to demonstrate is an economy that grows fast enough to cut poverty and sells more abroad — an issue that cannot be put off much longer.
Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

title: Legal remedies
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
THE missing persons’ issue is not new. The post-Soviet political tumult in the world released the pent-up energy of ethnic and ideological conflicts that had lain dormant under the stabilising hold of totalitarianism.
Consequently, as armed conflicts amongst and within nations intensified, the number of missing persons remained high during the mid-1990s. An international commission for missing persons was established in 1996 to track and resolve the issue in Yugoslavia’s conflict. The commission’s mandate was expanded in 2003 to include the global issues of missing persons in various conflicts, natural disasters, and climate migrations. 
The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance was signed in 2006, which defined enforced disappearance as “the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the state or by persons or groups of persons acting with the authorisation, support or acquiescence of the state”. The treaty entered into force in 2010.
The missing persons issue got further traction with the rise of ideologically inspired waves of terrorism by organisations like Al Qaeda, IS and several others. UNSC resolutions 1267, 1998, and 2253 established a list of terrorist entities including Al Qaeda, the Taliban, and IS to sanction these along with their financiers. Despite these international efforts, the domestic legal options to deal with terrorist entities remained fragmented. As a consequence, the issue of missing persons was conflated with the issue of enforced disappearances. 
Our low terrorism prosecution rate signals dysfunction.
It is difficult to separate voluntary and enforced disappearances globally. In Pakistan, a Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances was established in 2011 which has dealt with 10,947 missing persons’ cases throughout Pakistan and has resolved 9,447 (86 per cent) cases.
When judicial prosecution of hardened criminals becomes ineffective, it can create incentives for law-enforcement agencies to resort to vigilante justice. This can further create space for allegations of enforced disappearances where apprehension of terrorism suspects is not immediately followed by prosecution. Due care needs to be taken to sift cases of voluntary disappearances, crime-related arrests, and terrorism-related detentions. Differential legal treatment and prosecution are required to avoid a predilection for non-legal remedies on the part of LEAs. Pakistan’s low terrorism prosecution rate (8pc) over the past two decades, compared with 88pc in the UK, 99pc in China and 99.9pc in Japan, signals a dysfunctional prosecution system.
The inordinate delays in prosecution and conviction of terrorists create space for their political supporters to exploit legal gaps and build victimhood narratives. In Balochistan, terrorist organisations have spawned a fear psychosis by abducting judges in order to stymie the prosecution process. A few examples include the assassination of justice Muhammad Noor Mesk­anzai, former chief justice of Balochistan High Court in Kharan in 2022, and killing of district and sessions judge Abdul Hakeem Kaka in Mastung in July 2026. 
The threat extends beyond judges, with around 50 CTD officials killed in Balochistan, while the driver of a law officer was shot when the officer was recording his statement concerning the July 2026 Ziarat terrorist attack in which 27 policemen were killed.
To tackle these challenges, the government has amended Pakistan’s Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) 1997 thro­u­gh the insertion of Section 11-EEEE that provides for ‘Prev­e­ntive Dete­ntion for Inquiry’, allowing detention for up to 90 days for inquiry, thereby pro­viding a legal mechanism for investigating terrorism suspects by collecting evidence before moving to prosecute them. 
The Anti-Terrorism (Balochistan Amendment) Act, 2025, incorporates the amended ATA, 1997, to the province, enabling LEAs and the judiciary to detain the accused for 90 days, while Section 21-AAA of the Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Act, 2026, provides protection to judges and witnesses.
Since the implementation of the new law in Balochistan, out of 90 detainees, five have been released where the allegations could not be established, while 40 have been referred for trial through faceless courts, demonstrating movement from preventive detention towards prosecution through a defined legal process.
All the above measures show the government’s resolve to extend the full range of legal remedies to LEAs and the judiciary to arrest, investigate, and prosecute the terrorists, with celerity, and in accordance with the law, bringing much-needed transparency and fairness to the whole process. 
The writer has a PhD from Nust.
rwjanj@hotmail.com
Published in Dawn, October 10th, 2026

title: Animal rights in Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Altamush SaeedEiraj Hassan)
content:
FOR almost as long as Pakistan has existed, the state has had one answer to stray dogs: kill them. Poison and bullets have been the tools, and rabies control the justification. Yet after decades of culling, dogs still roam our streets, bite cases keep coming, and children still die of a disease that is entirely preventable.
That contradiction is now being argued in court, and the arguments are producing something larger than a verdict on dogs. Over the past two years, our courts have begun to treat the welfare of animals as a constitutional question. Pakistan may be witnessing the birth of a new branch of law.
There is a precedent for this. Environmental law in Pakistan was shaped less by legislation than by judges, who recognised that the right to life under Article 9 means more than bare survival and includes the right to a healthy environment. Driven in large part by the work of Dr Parvez Hassan in the Shehla Zia case, that jurisprudence turned ecology into a matter of fundamental rights. Animal law is now following the same path, and for similar reasons.
The World Health Organisation is clear that dog-mediated rabies is eliminated by vaccinating dogs, not by killing them. Mass vaccination, combined with humane population control through trap-neuter-vaccinate-return (TNVR), breaks the chain of transmission. Culling does not: it leaves gaps that unvaccinated dogs quickly fill, so the population and the disease both bounce back. Punjab recognised as much when it adopted an Animal Birth Control (TNVR) Policy. The trouble is that municipal authorities kept on culling anyway.
Animal law is not simply about preventing cruelty, but also about public health, biodiversity and good governance.
That gap between policy and practice is what brought Eiraj Hassan vs Government of Punjab, which one of us filed, to the Lahore High Court. The petition secured interim protection against illegal culling across the province, followed by directions that the policy be implemented in letter and spirit. The argument was taken further in Nelofar vs Chief Commissioner ICT, where principles of humane population management and animal sentience were developed. Read alongside the Islamabad High Court’s recognition of animal sentience in the Kaavan case, these rulings form an emerging body of law that treats animals as living beings whose welfare is bound with the health of society, not as property or pests.
The constitutional basis is not hard to find. Articles 9, 9A and 14 protect life and dignity, and our courts have long held that environmental degradation and threats to public health can violate both. Animal welfare belongs in the same frame. Wildlife trafficking, inhumane food systems, badly managed animal populations and the spread of zoonotic disease all bear directly on human health. The global public health community calls this ‘One Health’: the well-being of people, animals and the environment cannot be separated. The pandemic taught that lesson at enormous cost.
There is also a public safety argument. Decades of criminological research show that cruelty to animals frequently coexists with domestic violence, child abuse, and other violent crime. Violence against the powerless rarely stays confined to one kind of victim. A legal system that takes animal cruelty seriously is better placed to protect vulnerable people too. Animal rights do not compete with human rights; they reinforce them.
Dogs are only the beginning. Public interest petitions have since been filed over illegally imported monkeys, lions kept in circuses and private zoos, endangered black bears used for entertainment, the condition of farm animals, regulation of animal carts, and the enforcement of slaughter laws, where better practice serves both animal welfare and the containment of zoonotic disease. Each case makes the same point in a different setting: animal law is not simply about preventing cruelty, but also about public health, biodiversity, and good governance.
The groundwork outside the courtroom matters as much. In January 2025, Pakistan’s first International Animal and Environmental Rights Conference brought more than 700 judges, lawyers, academics and activists together with international organisations working in the field. It treated animal law not as a matter of charity but as a serious legal discipline. Kinnaird College in Lahore now teaches courses on animal rights law and food legal systems, and a new generation of lawyers is taking up this work.
But courts can only go so far. Judgements set principles; governments must turn them into practice. Punjab, which already has the right policy on paper, should fund TNVR programmes properly, train municipal staff, and hold officials accountable when culling continues in defiance of court orders. Other provinces and the federal capital should follow. Legislators should look again at a cruelty law that dates back to 1890 and at the patchy regulation of zoos, circuses and the wildlife trade. Universities and bar associations should keep building the expertise that litigation alone cannot supply.
If that happens, the past two years may be remembered not merely as a run of important cases, but as the moment Pakistan’s legal system began to take animals seriously. Environmental law changed how we understand our relationship with nature. Animal law can do the same for our relationship with the creatures we share it with. A society that protects its most vulnerable living beings is, in the end, a more just society for everyone in it.
Altamush Saeed is a lawyer who holds an LLM in animal law & environmental law and teaches animal law and food law at Kinnaird College, Lahore. Eiraj Hassan is a social media manager for the PSL at the Pakistan Cricket Board.
Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

title: Pakistan’s Yemen moment
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
ON Oct 5, in an emergency meeting, the member states of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement invoked the joint defence clause. Now, Islamabad and Ankara can actively move towards rapid force deployment to protect Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. The Middle East is one of the most complex and conflict-prone regions. The decision to operationalise the collective defence clause in less than two months of signing the MJDA suggests that Islamabad might remain embroiled in several layers of Middle Eastern conflicts in future under these security commitments. 
This is a classic Pakistan-Yemen moment, which the previous PML-N government avoided in 2015. Saudi Arabia officially asked Pakistan in 2015 to join its coalition against Yemen’s Houthis. However, Pakistan chose to remain neutral. More than a decade after Pakistan took one of its toughest foreign policy decisions, the Yemen moment has resurfaced. This time, however, Pakistan has made security commitments to Saudi Arabia under the MJDA in 2026 and the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed last year. 
Yemen is one of the most complex cases of civil unrest and conflict, illustrating how external actors can complicate regional and domestic conflict dynamics. Following a Saudi-led coalition’s seven-year intervention from 2015 to 2022, the UN brokered a truce. However, a final peace agreement remains pending. Consequently, until a formal Saudi-Houthi accord is finalised, Pakistan alongside Ankara may face prolonged military deployments lasting months or even years to bolster Saudi defence forces within their territory.
Despite these operational challenges, Pakistan must fulfil its security commitments to Saudi Arabia. In the realm of global geopolitics, a nation’s security commitments are the bedrock of its external power projection and diplomatic leverage. Having formally elevated its bilateral arrangements into the binding, Nato-like collective security framework of the MJDA, Islamabad cannot afford to hesitate when the pact is invoked. Therefore, Pakistan must fulfil its security obligations wholeheartedly to safeguard its strategic credibility. Furthermore, the economic dimension of this relationship underpins Pakistan’s very survival. Saudi Arabia has historically stood as Islamabad’s premier economic anchor during its darkest balance-of-payments and liquidity crises. 
To survive a perilous geopolitical tightrope, Pakistan must immediately execute a sophisticated, active, and dual-front diplomatic strategy.
While Islamabad must deliver on its collective defence commitment to Saudi Arabia, it cannot afford a catastrophic fallout with its western neighbour, Iran. Pakistan shares a volatile, 900-kilometre border with Iran, a frontier already plagued by cross-border militancy and fragile security dynamics. Direct military entanglement with the Iranian ‘Axis of Resistance’, or an operational misstep that Tehran perceives as hostile, would trigger an asymmetric blowback along the Balochistan border, destabilise Pakistan’s internal security, and ruin vital regional trade prospects. To survive this perilous geopolitical tightrope, Pakistan must immediately execute a sophisticated, active, and dual-front diplomatic strategy.
The first pillar of this strategy requires active diplomatic engagement with Iran to negotiate a comprehensive, long-term peace treaty between Riyadh and Tehran. By signing or even negotiating a peace treaty between the two capitals, Islamabad will likely be able to reduce regional tensions and minimise concerns of direct military confrontation under the MJDA with Iran. 
Islamabad is uniquely positioned for this role. Recently, Islamabad garnered significant diplomatic goodwill by acting as a trusted backchannel and mediator between the US and Iran. Islamabad’s mediatory role brought the US and Iran directly to the negotiating table, which culminated in the Islamabad MoU. However, given the immense scale of the current regional mistrust, hostilities, and crisis, Pakistan cannot walk this path alone. To maximise the probability of success, Islamabad must integrate China into a co-mediatory process.
This joint Beijing-Islamabad peace initiative can offer the perfect synergy of regional solutions for regional tensions. China has been viewed as a factor of stability in South Asia and the Middle East. While Pakistan possesses deep, institutionalised defence ties with Riyadh, and a shared diplomatic vocabulary with Tehran, China enjoys immense economic influence over both nations through its Belt and Road Initiative, and comprehensive strategic partnership agreement with Iran. Beijing has already demonstrated its diplomatic capability by successfully brokering the historic Saudi-Iran normalisation pact in 2023. By combining Islamabad’s strategic clout with China’s economic heft, this collaborative framework can offer Riyadh and Tehran structural security guarantees and economic incentives, respectively. These two elements can transform a fragile status quo into a durable, written peace treaty.
The second, equally critical pillar of Pakistan’s diplomatic strategy demands the immediate establishment of robust, direct, and uninterrupted communication channels between Islamabad and Tehran. As the MJDA moves from a paper agreement to rapid, physical deployment on the ground, the risk of miscalculation and misinterpretation of certain actions escalates exponentially. In a highly securitised environment, defensive posturing can easily be misconstrued as preparation for an offensive strike. Pakistan must institutionalise a permanent, high-level military-to-military and intelligence-sharing hotline with Iran. This will help Islamabad and Tehran curb disinformation campaigns by adversarial third parties or non-state actors that want to drive a wedge between Pakistan and Iran.
For years, Islamabad aspired to balance its relationship between Saudi Arabia and Iran. Perhaps Pakistan’s Yemen moment has arrived to test this balancing approach. Pakistan’s true value to both Riyadh and the broader Gulf region lies in its unique capacity to act as a credible, neutral mediator between the GCC and Iran. Pakistan cannot afford to back off from its defence commitments to Riyadh, but equally, it cannot afford to strain its ties with Tehran. Therefore, Islamabad’s Yemen moment should not damage its credibility as a defence partner of Saudi Arabia, nor create rifts with its important neighbour, Iran.
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: Listening before legislating
author: none@none.com (Ayesha Irshad Mian)
content:
EVERY World Mental Health Day arrives with a theme, a hashtag, and a flurry of panels. This year’s call to centre the voices of people with lived experience deserves more than a single day. It requires an honest accounting of whose voices have shaped our mental health agenda, and whose have been absent from it.
In clinical practice, one learns that people rarely describe their distress in the language of diagnosis. Recent events shape, and at times fortify, age-old dogmas. A young woman laments that recent allegations of sexual assault on a university campus have reinforced the view for her parents that places of learning are not safe for girls and that she must rethink her dreams. A teenage boy says he has not cried since he was nine, because he learned early what crying would cost him. A man in his 40s says he cannot tell his family he has stopped sleeping, because the word ‘depression’ would be heard as weakness, or worse, as madness. None of them is describing a disorder alone. Each is describing a world, and a mind adapting to it.
Mental health does not reside only within individuals. It is shaped by homes, classrooms, workplaces, streets, and the narratives a society sustains about who may be safe, who may be vulnerable, and who may speak. Pakistan ranks near the bottom of global gender parity indices; millions of girls remain out of school. When women fear pursuing an education, or when their aspirations are quietly renegotiated, the consequences extend well beyond the economic. They appear as hopelessness, chronic anxiety, and a constriction of possibility. Boys raised to equate emotion with weakness and dominance with worth bear a different burden: silence, aggression turned inward or outward, and little vocabulary for distress. Patriarchy shapes the psychological lives of every gender.
Stigma compounds this. Mental illness is still widely seen as a moral failing, a spiritual affliction, a source of family shame. Public awareness of what depression, anxiety, psychosis, or trauma actually involves — and that they are treatable — is limited. People wait for years before seeking care, often turning first to faith healers, informal practitioners, or no one at all. Many of us carry a sense of heaviness at how slowly some things change. It is worth naming that feeling rather than suppressing it. Despair can be worked through collectively.
On this World Mental Health Day and beyond, people with lived experience must be heard.
Against this backdrop, the launch of the national mental health policy on Oct 1 was a necessary step. A policy places mental health on the public agenda, gives advocates a reference point, and offers the system a direction. The political will behind it must be acknowledged. A launch, however, is a moment, whereas implementation is the work of a decade. Pakistan has over 250 million people. By most estimates, it has roughly 500 psychiatrists and a comparable number of psychologists, with no licensing body to regulate the practice of psychology, and, therefore, no uniform standard of training, scope, or accountability. The scarcity is sharper still in specialist areas. There are fewer than 10 child and adolescent psychiatrists in the country, and child psychologists are almost non-existent. Mental health has been under-resourced for decades.
This is not a criticism of any individual or institution. It is the arithmetic of a neglected field, with far-reaching consequences. Where specialists are scarce, implementation tends to fall on others: dedicated NGOs, short-course trainees, and well-intentioned professionals who have not had the opportunity to work with many patients over many years, often without regular supervision. Nuanced, effective mental healthcare rests on the clinical judgement to distinguish grief from depression, trauma from defiance, and a cry for help from a pattern of behaviour that signals something more. That judgement is built through years of practice, mentorship, error corrected under guidance, and slow accumulation of patients’ stories. Without it, even well-designed programmes can overlook those most in need.
The need for distinction is greater still given the context. Pakistan contends with floods and heatwaves, economic precarity, displacement, gender-based violence, and the effects of regional conflict — among the principal determinants of mental health. Implementation in such conditions requires people who understand both the science and the street.
As we welcome the policy, and look forward to its implementation, some principles deserve consideration.
Implementation is best guided by practitioners with long front-line clinical and research experience in the country, supported by public health and systems expertise. Second, a rigorous, costed strategic plan is essential. The design must specify which services will be delivered in which districts, by whom, under whose supervision, and measured against what indicators. Aspiration must be translated into sequence and budget. Third, this must be directed by a coalition of experts. Psychiatrists, psychologists, mental health researchers, paediatricians, educators, social workers, legal experts, and people with lived experience should work at one table rather than in silos. Fourth, funding must match the stated priority. Whether through government allocation or philanthropy, sustained investment in training, supervision, public awareness, and a licensing framework for psychologists is what converts intention into infrastructure. Expanding the specialist pipeline, from child and adolescent services to adult care, would be transformative.
International expertise is valuable, and Pakistan will continue to benefit from shared learning. Yet the durability of any approach depends on its fit with local realities: the district hospital, the crowded clinic, the family weighing in insistent on joint management and care, the need for task shifting, etc. Those who practise here, and who remain once project cycles end, understand that terrain best. If this year’s theme is to be taken seriously, clinicians and communities on the ground belong at the centre of this work and at the helm of it, not at its margins. Above all, people with lived experience must be heard. The woman who wants to study, the boy who wants permission to feel, and the adult who has suffered silently for years are telling us what they need: safety, dignity, and to be believed. No policy will succeed if it is written about them rather than with them. 
On this World Mental Health Day, we might resolve to build a system as thoughtful as the people it is meant to serve. The policy is a promise. Keeping it will require patience, expertise, and humility. 
The writer is a consultant child, adolescent and adult psychiatrist and founder & CEO at Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute.

title: Vanished girls
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE scourge of female disappearances in Pakistan should be a matter of shame. Institutional reforms and criminalising chauvinistic traditions remain long overdue measures. The Lahore High Court, during the hearing of a case of disappearance, was informed by Punjab’s police chief that over 500 cases of girls reported missing were still pending in the province. The figure was shocking for the court. Not only was concern expressed at the ordeal of the families of the missing, the negligence of police was also underscored in this regard. Chief Justice Aalia Neelum inquired about mechanisms to tackle cases involving women and children. The IGP stated that such incidents would be handled by special committees.
The crisis of our ‘missing’ daughters has detrimental repercussions for victims. Those recovered are forced to live with multiple accusations from their kin who often suspect sexual exploitation. Many fall prey to sex trafficking and are sold to organised prostitution networks, or are registered as kidnap cases when they run away to escape forced marriages. As most of them hail from poor areas and families, the authorities often dismiss their kidnappings as ‘elopement’, without any investigation. That it takes various court orders for police to pursue these abductions implies gross apathy, negligence, and the absence of accountability. For years, adequate action to arrest the trend in the rural and urban areas of the province, and the lack of protection for victims who return or are rescued against the tag of ‘dishonour’, have been non-existent. It is time these cases were also seen as part of the thriving sex trafficking rings in the country. In 2022, police figures showed that 3,571 abducted girls and women were missing across Punjab; a total of 40,585 women were kidnapped between 2017 and January 2022. Keeping the girl child safe entails going beyond reasons of domestic dispute and investigating prolonged disappearances as possible cases of trafficking.

title: Let them eat cake
author: none@none.com (Aasim Sajjad Akhtar)
content:
YET another World Bank report has been published highlighting the unending immiseration of Pakistan’s working people. Pakistan’s economic plight is described as largely on par with war-torn countries in the Arab region like Syria and Yemen. Unsurprisingly, the bank makes only limited mention of its own role in relentlessly enforcing the ‘structural adjustment’ policies which have greatly contributed to mass impoverishment. But the report is damning nonetheless.
Almost 20 per cent of Pakistan’s 260 million people now fall into the extreme-poor category, defined as a daily income of less than $3. Extreme poverty has increased three-fold in less than a decade. If the poverty line is simulated at the slightly higher daily income level of $4.20, almost half of Pakistan’s people are poor. It is not all doom and gloom, of course, because Pakistani capitalists, landlords, and state mafias are doing very well. This is reflected in inequality markers. What economists call the Gini coefficient is at its highest level in almost 40 years.
The report goes on to name a series of ‘shocks’ which have triggered the huge uptick in poverty; the Covid pandemic and the 2022 floods top the list. Missing is a meaningful political economy analysis in which class exploitation, colonial statecraft, and aid dependency are accorded the centrality that our sordid experience demands. In a nutshell, Pakistan’s masses are the targets of a scandalous class war that becomes more intense with each passing day. The main protagonists of this war are Pakistan’s own militarised ruling class and its external patrons, including the World Bank, IMF and bilateral ‘partners’.
Even where the World Bank report notes that rising poverty and inequality is partly the result of a “prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities”, the mention of the actual players that push the adjustment agenda is conspicuous by its absence. And there is nothing about Pakistan’s own state mafias, capitalists and landed magnates who happily pass on spiralling debt burdens to the people, whilst profiting endlessly through real estate and trade, with no concern for livelihoods and ecologies.
Working families are eating less on the whole.
There have been donor reports, which go beyond superficially describing social crises and actually name some names. In 2020, the UNDP’s annual Pakistan National Human Development Report explicitly stated that Pakistan’s militarised ruling class benefits from hidden — and sometimes overt — subsidies to the tune of $17.4 billion per annum. Six years later, one can assume that this figure has grown; it is another matter that donors are seemingly unwilling to name the protagonists of this class war as explicitly now as in 2020.
The truth deficit extends to our own political classes and intelligentsia. Yes, one could argue that ‘elite capture’ has become a widely used phrase. Petrol bombs and other markers of inflation come in for regular criticism and parties like the Jamaat-i-Islami are given licence to undertake sanitised protests. But the political and intellectual mainstream is least concerned with the banality of everyday class war in comparison to intra-elite palace intrigues and diplomatic ‘successes’ in the geopolitical realm.
Indeed, mainstream political conflict in Pakistan features only shades of the right, and the object of politics is to secure the good graces of the establishment, which in turn continues to rely on the age-old policy of securing geostrategic rents from external patrons. It is thus that the mass of Pakistan’s people has been thrust further down the class ladder for at least a decade, and arguably longer. Throughout this period, the actual political-economic order has remained largely unchanged, irr­espective of who has occupied the formal seat of government.
The accumulation of crises has made the present moment particularly desperate. The ruling regime proclaims its macroeconomic achievements while promising that the windfalls of its great accomplishments abroad will materialise soon. But the statistics that they do not advertise tell the real story. Working families are eating less on the whole and even less nutritiously than before; kids are pulled out of school and forced to work to supplement meagre household incomes; even those who imagine themselves as white-collar workers, let alone those who are in the category of extreme poor, contemplate killing themselves and their offspring to preserve their dignity.
It is thus that one is reminded of the 18th-century ‘French princess’ to whom the reply ‘let them eat cake’ was attributed, when her advisers explained that the mass of her subjects were not able to afford bread. The French Revolution followed some years later.
The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.

title: Moscow disagreement
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE fact that a consensus on how to deal with terrorism originating in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan eludes regional states was made clear at the recently held Moscow Format moot. The event was attended by nearly all of Afghanistan’s neighbours, including Pakistan. However, there was no joint statement issued because, in the words of the Russian envoy for Afghanistan, “our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn’t see eye to eye”. The Taliban regime had also sent its representatives. The main sticking point was the Taliban’s objection to including Afghanistan in a “terrorist context”. However, as Pakistan’s envoy put it, it was essential to address “the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil”. Russia offered its good offices to help de-escalate matters between Kabul and Islamabad, though it noted that the Moscow Format was not a forum for resolving bilateral disputes.
Both the Taliban’s denialism, and Russia’s apparently soft stance towards the Afghan terrorism problem, are unfortunate. Groups that find shelter in Afghanistan under the Taliban threaten the entire region. Thus, all of Afghanistan’s neighbours need to speak with one voice regarding the ‘export’ of terrorism. Russia is the only state that recognises the Taliban regime. Moscow has its own reasons for indulging the Taliban; these include the need to fight IS-K, which is a common enemy of Russia and the Taliban rulers, as well as to check US and Western influence in Afghanistan. But engagement with Kabul must not be allowed to obscure the fact that some of the deadliest terrorist groups in the world find refuge on Afghan soil. Other regional forums, such as the SCO and the ECO, have highlighted the need to address the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. China, which has significant economic interests in Afghanistan, has also pointed to this terrorist threat. The UN Security Council, too, has frequently noted that Afghanistan under Taliban rule has once again become a haven for various terrorist groups. Pakistan’s insistence, therefore, that Afghanistan’s terrorism problem be highlighted reflects the reality of the situation. If Kabul addresses the issue sincerely and restrains terrorist groups, it will benefit not only the Afghan people but the entire region.

title: Midterm break
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AMERICAN President Donald Trump’s statement that he will not launch a fresh attack on Iran before the US midterm elections does little to calm fears of renewed war in the Gulf. In effect, the US president has only promised to postpone the attack, when he should have committed to indefinitely suspending hostilities in favour of dialogue. Clearly, it is a calculated political move: the Iran war is unpopular with the American people, mainly because of the inflation and high petroleum prices it has caused. Mr Trump may be holding off on a new assault to prevent a complete drubbing of the Republicans at the ballot box. What is perplexing is the mixed messaging. While refusing to rule out a post-midterms attack, he also said that the Iran war was going to end “very soon”. Most observers have lost count of how many times he has said this. He added that talks with Tehran were “productive”. Should the world believe that a new attack is imminent after the US elections? Or is the US looking to wind things down? Perhaps those calling the shots in Washington themselves do not know. It is also a matter of concern that Israel is reportedly contemplating another attack on Iran. 
Both the US and Israel need to halt their destructive misadventures in the Middle East. Their irresponsible warmongering has resulted in widespread bloodshed across the region and has upended the global economy. Washington and Tehran have exchanged proposals on how to end the conflict. Mr Trump and his cohorts, therefore, need to concentrate exclusively on the diplomatic track, instead of fuelling speculation regarding fresh hostilities. Already, the Yemen conflict is spiralling out of control. If the US and Israel were to spark another round of violence with Iran, the consequences for the entire region — indeed the world at large — would be grim. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is already constrained. If Bab al-Mandeb were also to be closed, and the export of petrochemicals from the region curtailed further because of conflict, the entire world will pay the price for the deadly follies of Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Therefore, instead of speaking in riddles, President Trump must commit his country to the peace process, offer the Iranians a fair deal, and bring his military home from the Middle East.

title: Public good and spaces
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
NINETY-FOUR per cent of youth had no access to a library, 93pc to a sports facility, and 78pc to a park. Ninety-seven per cent had never been to a live music event, 94pc to a sports event, and 97pc to the cinema. A whopping 71pc had no access to any of the above. These figures are from a survey conducted for UNDP’s Pakistan National Human Development Report 2017: Unleashing the potential of a young Pakistan, of which Dr Adil Najam and I were the lead authors. It was a national survey that highlighted a youth population with few opportunities for positive engagement outside their home.
Since 2017, the economy has not been doing well. We have not had any significant positive changes in national human development outcomes, and the impact of Covid and global slowdown has hardly been encouraging. So, one would expect that since conditions have not changed much, a similar survey carried out today would show numbers that are not very different from those reported then.
I have been staying in London for the last couple of months. There is a large park about 400 metres away from our place. The park is managed by the local council (local government). It has a walking/ jogging track running along its almost kilometre-long perimeter. The park has two multipurpose fields. I saw them being used as cricket fields in August and they were converted into football and rugby fields in September. There are three hard-surface tennis courts on one side. There is a children’s play area with lots of structures to climb, swing from, and slide on. The play area is full most evenings.
The park is utilised well. Hundreds of children, parents, and dogs visit it every day. Walkers, dog-walkers — most of whom pick up their pet’s poop themselves — and joggers are there round the clock. The tennis courts, play area, and fields get busy in the afternoon after school on weekdays. They are occupied throughout the day on weekends. Every afternoon, four to five groups of young people, with their coaches, have training sessions in the park. There are always cricket or football matches going on. On weekends, quite a few groups have picnics there too. The park is, of course, open to all.
We have not had any significant positive changes in national human development outcomes.
It would not be an overstatement to say that the park defines the neighbourhood and its vibe. It is a very family-oriented area and one sees that parents are comfortable allowing their young children to run around the park or ride their bike or scooters around the jogging track — often unsupervised. A lot of credit for this goes to the local council. The park does require significant upkeep for cleaning and maintaining the track, trees and plants, and the grassy fields. But, since residents can benefit from healthy activities, the council provides the needed services quite diligently.
Walking down our area’s high street takes us to the local public library, which is also run by the local council. Since we are a family of readers, and buying books is not cheap, we went in to check if we could be members of the local library. All it took was proof of residence in the area to obtain membership cards free of cost. We then had access to not just the local library but all public libraries around the council (six, I think). One person can borrow up to 20 books at a time for up to three weeks. If a book is not available at our library, we can request it from other libraries in the network that have it. Over the last two weeks, my daughter has read six to seven books. Imagine the saving! And she has had fun learning and managing her own library membership card as well as the activity of borrowing and returning books. I am a little worried that the speed at which she is going, she might not have much left to read at the library in a month or two!
Providing access to books is just a small part of the services on offer. The library has very inviting spaces for sitting and reading, and even desks for writing. It has free Wi-Fi and free access to internet-connected desktops for members. It also has at-cost facilities for printing and photocopying, and a decently priced cafeteria. There are also some rooms and spaces that can be booked for group activities. I have seen language-learning, meditation, and book-discussion clubs using these spaces. It has been a bit of a surprise to see a broad cross-section of society using these facilities. The book section for the young is always bustling. And from teenagers to retirees, all age groups are well represented throughout the day at the library.
The local council provides all these public spaces. Local accountability for local issues seems to work well here. It is difficult to list all the benefits that accrue to the citizens from these two spaces and the free services that come with them. There are opportunities for physical, mental, and emotional engagement through group activities, social interaction, reading and learning, and hobbies and interests. It is important for all people to have such opportunities for these healthy activities, so that they can interact positively and learn to work together, and, generally, become engaged citizens. The contrast between where we need to be and the findings of the survey of Pakistani youth mentioned earlier could not be starker.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.

title: Chain of custody
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
LAST month, at the London School of Economics’ Environment Week, the International Growth Centre asked a roundtable of policymakers, researchers and funders how evidence systems should change to support harder climate choices. I opened with a case: a major climate decision Pakistan took without the evidence it needed.
The obvious case is the 2022 floods. The obvious diagnosis is that the evidence did not exist. The case is obviously right. The diagnosis is obviously wrong.
When a third of the country went under water, every decision that followed, from evacuation to the Geneva appeal, was taken in the dark. Yet the Met department had forecast an above-normal monsoon. The national socio-economic registry held geo-coded records on 38 million households. River and satellite data sat with Wapda, the Federal Flood Commission and Suparco. The knowledge existed, in different buildings. No one was mandated to bring it to the table.
Pakistan does not have a data shortage. The usual verdict is poor coordination. That is the wrong word. Coordination is voluntary. What Pakistan lacks is a chain of custody: someone legally obliged to carry evidence to the point of decision.
The five federal agencies that hold hazard data share no protocol.
The roundtable framed three tensions: whether evidence serves the decisions governments actually take, whether it arrives in time to be used, and whether it supports implementation or only design. In Pakistan, each tension marks a break in that chain. Each break has a price tag.
Evidence and decision: Pakistan’s research agenda follows what funders find easy to finance, not what the state must prioritise. A warning system has four parts: knowing the risk, forecasting it, getting the message out, and making people act on it. Since before the 2022 floods, the money has gone to the first two. Radars can be procured, counted and inaugurated. Dissemination and response are institutional work. They are not as lucrative as procurement tenders.
Nor has the state compiled basic baselines: tested district plans, embankment condition, maintenance costs. That absence is political economy. The reason is elite capture: new schemes bring contracts, win constituencies and visibility. Maintenance brings none.
Speed and usability: Pakistan models slowly what it needs fast and leaves its fastest evidence unconnected. The five federal agencies that hold hazard data share no protocol. In Buner in August 2025, a red alert was in force and households still did not move. No one told them what to do, and local governments had no assigned role in last-mile delivery. An SMS that says a flood is coming is information, not a warning for immediate action.
The BISP registry is a simpler case. Laid over hazard maps, it could tell a provincial authority within hours who stands in the path of a surge and how to pay them. It is the most decision-ready evidence Pakistan owns. It costs nothing new to produce. Usable evidence in Pakistan rarely needs a better model. It needs a legal duty to share and an interface between databases that already exist.
Implementation and capability: This is where costs are highest and evidence thinnest. After 2022, cash transfers were the state’s fastest instrument. They reached only households already on the registry. Exclusion ran to a third in some districts, and nearly half the unregistered did not know how to register. The design was sound. No one was tasked with the evidence that would have exposed the gap during delivery.
Damage assessment has no owner either. No platform links damage to recovery, and there is no loss and damage registry. The 2022 needs assessment was built for the Geneva appeal, not the reconstruction. Pakistan chaired the G77 when the loss and damage fund was agreed at COP27. A country that cannot document its losses will struggle to draw on the fund it fought to create.
After the 18th Amendment, disaster management and irrigation are provincial; hydromet data, the registry and international finance are federal. Evidence must cross that line twice: up for financing, down for delivery. When a donor project closes, its capability leaves with it, because the analysts sat in a project unit, not a line department with a budget head.
The cost of moving blind: These are not administrative inefficiencies. They are why Pakistan’s development agenda is now set by its flood cycle rather than its plans. The 2010, 2022 and 2025 floods each erased growth, reopened IMF negotiations and diverted development money into rehabilitation and reconstruction. Every rupee spent rebuilding what better evidence could have protected is a rupee taken from schools, clinics and the investment that would shrink the next shock. The logic is simple: the Global Commission on Adaptation estimates that 24 hours’ warning of a coming storm can cut the damage by 30pc.
High-tech or grassroots: My notes for the roundtable ended with a question for funders: should a country like Pakistan invest in predictive modelling or in grassroots readiness? It is a false choice. The answer is sequence. Better models will lengthen lead times and should be pursued. But a 72-hour forecast is worthless to a household off the registry, in a town with no local government, receiving a non-specific message. The next rupee should buy a messenger, not a model.
Moving forward: Three steps, in sequence.
First, assign ownership. Notify a binding data-sharing protocol across federal and provincial agencies, and name one owner for assessment data. Informal sharing must become a legal duty.
Second, connect what exists before the next monsoon. Link the registry to hazard maps in every province. Compile the missing baselines and open a loss and damage registry. Give local governments a formal role in warnings.
Third, commission evidence to decisions. Funders, including those around that table in London, should finance all four parts of the warning chain, not the two that are easiest to procure, and embed analysts in provincial departments under budget heads that outlive the project.
Pakistan does not lack evidence. It lacks a chain of custody. Until someone is responsible for carrying knowledge to the point of decision, every flood will end with the same verdict: the data existed, and no one was duty-bound to use it.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, October 8th, 2026

title: Broken people
author: none@none.com (Naeem Sadiq)
content:
TWO sanitation workers, 17-year-old Vanesh and 35-year-old Ramesh, tragically died while cleaning an underground tank at a building in Bhimpura, Karachi, on Sept 10. These deaths occurred exactly in the same manner and for exactly the same reason as the deaths that occur week after week in the sewage gutters of Pakistan. Cruelly exploited sanitation workers, compelled by poverty, are made to enter raw gutters to clean faecal matter with their bare hands, under barbaric and inhumane conditions. Some never come out alive. Those who make it back to the surface emerge with bruises, cuts and wounds with the filth having permeated not just their bodies, but their entire existence.
More than two dozen sanitation workers have died in sewage gutters across Pakistan this year. They were unknown privately contracted individuals, not listed as employees of any organisation. No individual or organisation was held accountable for gross criminal negligence. The families of the deceased were silenced by giving a few thousand rupees to sign a certificate that they shall not pursue any legal action. The unconcerned state looked the other way, as if nothing ever happened. There were no investigations, no FIRs, nor any compensation. Those who caused these deaths continued to live a life of luxury and were never held accountable.
In a landmark judgment delivered on Aug 13, 2026, the Bombay High Court declared that the families of deceased sanitation workers would be compensated by the state or the government agency, even if the death occurred because of work undertaken by a private contractor. This direction unequivocally places the compensation obligation on government entities and not private employers, thus protecting vulnerable families from running after the reluctant private entities for compensation. The court also determined the compensation value at Rs30 lakhs per deceased worker.
How come no one in Pakistan questioned the fact that none of the two dozen sanitation workers who died this year were employees of the government departments who are paid billions to do this job. Should we not ask as to why we have parked highly paid managing directors in dysfunctional organisations such as Karachi or Hyderabad Water and Sewerage Corporations or the Water and Sanitation Agencies of Punjab? Why does no one in Pakistan question the uncomfortable paradox: how come all those who died were non-Muslims?
Vulnerable citizens cannot be left to die because of negligence.
Globally, the practice of sending workers into sewerage systems for cleaning and desilting has been largely eliminated and replaced by mechanised equipment and modern technologies. Several countries including India have also enacted legal prohibitions against such practices, recognising them as incompatible with human dignity and occupational safety. Pakistan today possesses both the technology and the capacity to adopt safer alternatives. Mechanical sewer-cleaning equipment is now readily available, while major utility organisations already possess fleets of mechanised cleaning vehicles.
Pakistan cannot continue to practise cruelty and inhumanity in dealing with its minorities and its most vulnerable citizens. They cannot be left to die because of the negligence, incompetence or criminal failure of individuals and organisations. A state that has achieved distinction in high-speed legislation can easily and urgently pass a bill that states: “No worker shall be required or permitted to enter sewage gutters, manholes, drains, or septic tanks for the purpose of cleaning, desilting, or removing blockages. Such activities shall be carried out through mecha­nical means and equipment.” Any order, instruction or permission to enter a sewage gutter for cleaning could be declared a cognizable offence, and the head of the organisation made to bear direct legal responsibility.
A nation with the slightest conscience, humanity or remorse must begin by legislating the above-mentioned prohibition and ordering a judicial inquiry to investigate all deaths that took place in the last one year. The state must register FIRs against the responsible organisations and individuals, even where a settlement was reached with the families of the deceased. If the families of Gul Plaza victims could be compensated by Rs10 million each, why can the state not exemplify the same generosity for its non-Muslim citizens? The adoption of these measures could demonstrate our nation’s forgotten commitment to human rights, occupational safety, and social justice. Must the healing of our most oppressed, brutalised and broken people not be our first step towards building a progressive Pakistan?

title: Talking about the exchange rate
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
THERE is an enduring consensus in Pakistan that the exchange rate should not be allowed to move by much as a matter of routine, and that determining its level is a matter of discretion for the state. In some areas we call this “Dar-o-nomics”, after Ishaq Dar, whose name came to be attached to exchange rate policy not because he invented it, but because he has been its most important and visible advocate. Otherwise this thinking dates back to Ghulam Ishaq Khan, who was of the mind that the state should liberalise the economy in such a way that it does not lose its commanding position as the arbiter of all economic outcomes. From deciding the exchange rate, to deciding who gets to make how much profit and what should be the normal indexed rate of return on private capital in the economy, GIK wanted a model of liberalisation that kept all these decisions firmly in the hands of the government.
Nowhere is this thinking more clearly stated, and perhaps to more devastating effect, than around how it treats the question of the exchange rate. Over the years many have given voice to this thinking in different ways, and their arguments cluster around three basic assertions. One, devaluations lead to a hike in the rupee-denominated debt service burden. Two, devaluations do nothing to boost exports, they only provide a short-lived impetus that is quickly frittered away as costs of imported inputs rise accordingly, and exporters are forced to pass the price benefit on to their buyers. Three, devaluation causes inflation that burdens the poor disproportionately.
None of these assertions is wrong. What is wrong, however, is deploying them in defence of a fixed exchange rate. What all those who have used these assertions over the years have failed to do is actually study Pakistan’s own episodes of exchange rate devaluation. Were they to do that, they would realise that devaluations in our own history have nothing to do with restoring export competitiveness or anything quite so grand. In truth, devaluations are forced upon us because the supply of dollars relative to the supply of rupees in the economy shrinks to a point where a mass stampede breaks out with everyone rushing for the exits. Devaluations have to be undertaken to reflect the new reality of supply and demand of FX liquidity, and to halt the stampede. That’s all.
To all those who want to talk about the exchange rate, I ask them to study three episodes from Pakistan’s own history when devaluations happened. The first was in 2007 and ran till late 2008. The second began in late 2017 and ran till 2019. The third episode began in the middle of 2021 and ran till the middle of 2023. These three cycles teach us everything we need to know about exchange rate management.
Devaluations in our own history have nothing to do with restoring export competitiveness or anything quite so grand.
Each episode happened when Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves were depleting fast in the face of skyrocketing import and debt service bills. In each episode the government chose to first hold the ground and finance the outflows using borrowed money. In each episode they hit a point where further financing was insufficient to meet the pace of the reserve erosion. And in each episode the government hit a point where they had no choice but to reprice the dollar to reflect the new reality of its supply versus demand.
In short, in each episode the government chose to drive blindly towards a cliff. So the question to ask is what they were telling themselves along the way. The pattern is the same every time. Reserves peak, the government of the day boasts about having built “record high reserves”, and then the trade deficit begins to swell. For a few months remittances cover the trade deficit so there is no urgency to act. Then the current account swings into deficit and remains there, and then the deficits begin to grow. The government borrows to replenish the reserves. The borrowing hits a limit, the current account deficit marches along, and reserve depletion accelerates.
What are they telling themselves during these times, when the pressure is mounting but has not yet reached catastrophic proportions? It has been my unpleasant duty to have covered all three of these cycles over the past two decades, and I can confirm that in each episode they tell themselves the same thing. First, that the current account deficits are temporary, or driven by one-off factors. When the reserve erosion begins to trigger a flight into the dollars, they argue that administrative measures are required to stem the outflows and bring stability back. When they are advised to reprice the dollar before things get out of hand, they respond that exchange rate adjustments do nothing to increase exports, while they produce harm for the country in the form of higher debt service bills and inflation.
Eventually they all succumb. They succumb for the simple reason that you cannot endlessly spend money that is not yours to spend. And when they succumb, they grumble and complain. But they never derive any lessons from what they have just lived through, and what they have just seen happen in front of their eyes.
What is it they say about those who fail to learn from their own history? They are doomed to repeat it. This is why we have been through this cycle three times already. And yet, today, one more time, we can see people in positions of power, once again, start to repeat the same old nonsense all over again. Once again people who have no idea of what Pakistan’s experience with the exchange rate has been are trying to build arguments on how to manage it. And once again, they are trotting out the same tired old tropes, thus setting the stage for round four of this unhappy roller coaster for yet one more ride.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: LIGO, not Lego
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
WE Pakistanis excel individually, but abroad. We fail collectively, at home. Our role models are either dead or live in self-exile.
The best among the best must be our first Nobel Laureate — Dr Abdus Salam. The son of a schoolteacher in Maghiana, a hamlet in Jhang district (Punjab), he won a scholarship to Government College, Lahore, at the precocious age of 14. He studied locally for another two years until he passed his FA exams, with unbeatably high marks.
His academic trajectory took him to Cambridge University and then into a higher empyrean when, in 1979, he won the Nobel Prize in physics. He placed its gold medal around the neck of his former teacher Anilendra Ganguly, the man who had inspired him to study mathematics. Dr Salam died in 1996, disillusioned and disappointed, a modern Socrates poisoned by the prejudice of his compatriots.
Other Pakistanis who have excelled are Dr Azra Raza, the famous Karachi-born oncologist who has made impressive strides in cancer research; Dr Salima Ikram, a leading Pakistan-born Egyptologist; and Dr Nergis Mavalvala, the renowned astrophysicist and currently dean, MIT’s School of Science.
Great minds testify to the capacity of the human brain.
Dr Azra Raza has done for cancer research and Urdu poetry what Marie Curie did for radium and radioactivity. To hear Dr Raza speak on her work, which she does but not often enough in Pakistan, is to learn how cancer can be arrested, often at source.
Had Dr Azra been born 5,000 years ago in ancient Egypt, she might have made the pharaohs concentrate more on preserving life rather than preparing vainly for an afterlife. Dr Salima Ikram’s studies in Egyptology deepen the digs into a civilisation that paralleled our own Indus Valley civilisation — but without the unguents, the rituals and the gilded funerary objects.
If 5,000 years into the past is a long time, Dr Nergis Mavalvala’s work takes us billions of light years away, into galaxies beyond ours. She was inspired by Einstein’s 1915 general theory of relativity, which described “space and time as something that can stretch and compress, rather than a fixed stage”. Einstein believed that “a violent enough event should send a disturbance rippling outward through space and time themselves”. He left it to future generations to measure those ripples, known as gravitational waves.
Dr Nergis, her mentor Dr Rainer Weiss (who won the Nobel Prize for physics in 2017) and their team pioneered the study of gravitational waves through the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) project. On Sept 14, 2015, LIGO scientists detected a signal that emanated from the collision and merger of two black holes, each about 30 times the mass of our sun. The signal came from 1.3 billion light years away. It lasted only a fraction of a second but was recordable.
Suddenly, man no longer needed a telescope to see the universe through light waves. These can suffer distortion. Purer gravitational waves captured on ultra-sophisticated equipment could be heard.
Subsequent improvements in LIGO’s instruments enabled scientists to announce last year that, after detecting over 300 such black hole mergers, they could confirm Einstein’s predictions and Dr Stephen Hawking’s theorem regarding black holes.
Dr Nergis, like all great minds, has the ability to compress complicated concepts into assimilable ideas. Many of her brilliantly simplified presentations are available at the click of a button on YouTube. Audiences in Karachi and Lahore were privileged to hear her in person recently. She spoke to them from an intellectual height, which is where their heads should have been.
Minds like hers which can comprehend infinite galaxies, billions of light years, millennia of history, or, like Mao Zedong, foresee centuries into the future, testify to the limitless capacity of the human brain.
Edgar Snow, in his Red Star over China, recalls Mao and his wife watching a moth give its life to a candle. Charmed by its win­­gs, “shaded a delicate apple-green frin­ged in a soft rainbow of saffron and rose”, Mao presses the lifeless gossamer of colour into a book. And, after the gruelling Long March, Mao composes a poem which ends: And then, the last pass vanquished, Three Armies smiled. Snow asks whether such people can be thinking seriously of war?
One is reminded of A.B. Vajpayee’s poem that he recited in Lahore: Hum jang na honay deynge, khoon ka rang na honay deynge. [We will not allow war, nor let its blood colour us.]
A human brain weighs 1.4kg, consists primarily (60pc) of fat, and contains 100 billion neurons. Imagine the waste, if the folly of one unthinking mind trumpeting war, pressed a button and annihilated our entire past, all our present, and the limitless possibilities inherent in our future.
The writer is an author.

title: Dual citizen? Debarred
author: none@none.com (Saeed Ahmed)
content:
IT was a Friday afternoon in May 2019. State Bank of Pakistan Governor Tariq Bajwa was in Islamabad with the IMF mission, flanked by his technical team I led. Unbeknownst to him, his successor was already in the country. By evening, Bajwa had resigned. The finance secretary at the time told me a new governor would be appointed by nightfall: Reza Baqir, the IMF’s resident representative in Egypt, already in town and ready to assume charge. The notification followed the next day, a Saturday. Within 24 hours, over a weekend, a serving IMF official had been installed at the helm of the central bank, as abruptly as Bajwa’s own 2017 appointment had followed a rupee devaluation.
Opacity is not the only problem; law compounds it. The 2022 amendments to the SBP Act, while granting welcome operational autonomy, also imposed restrictions found nowhere in the IMF’s own safeguards assessment: an outright bar on dual nationals, and a requirement that a candidate completes a full five-year term before turning 65. Together, these eliminate precisely the cohort best placed to lead the central bank, favouring insiders over competence.
Contrast this with how Britain appoints the governor of the Bank of England: open international advertisement, a shortlist, ministerial interviews, and months of public notice before the transition begins. That is the process that produced Andrew Bailey to succeed Mark Carney in March 2020. In Pakistan, favoured candidates are installed within a day, while everyone else waits months, even years, for a vacancy the law says must be filled within 30 days.
Mark Carney’s trajectory sharpens the point further. A Canadian citizen who also held Irish citizenship through family ancestry, he was appointed governor of the Bank of England in Nov 2012, and ran UK monetary policy and financial stability for nearly seven years, through the 2016 Brexit shock. In 2018, while still governor, he acquired British citizenship too, holding three nationalities as custodian of Britain’s currency, with no credible case that he favoured Canadian or Irish interests over British ones.
Central banking is one of the few institutions where competence, not compliance, should be the only test.
Stanley Fischer, author of three of the most influential economics textbooks, and former first deputy managing director of the IMF, served as vice chair of the US Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2017, while holding two citizenships, from age 70 to 74.
More recently, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand appointed Dr Anna Breman, a Swedish national, as its first female governor. Dr Breman’s appointment in Aug 2025 followed a rigorous recruitment process, that even involved a global executive search firm.
Baqir is the more contested recent case, but the criticism was never really about a passport; it was that an IMF insider negotiating a Pakistani programme sat ‘on both sides of the table’, a concern about institutional capture, not nationality.
The consequences have been predictable. The governor’s post fell vacant in May 2022 and took over three months to fill, breaching the SBP Act’s 30-day requirement; a deputy governor’s post vacant since Nov 2024 was filled only in Aug 2026. Leadership has increasingly gone to candidates with modest qualifications, and qualified economists are either sidelined or leaving the SBP, a brain drain that is entirely self-inflicted. Brain drain is estimated to cost Pakistan roughly $4.2 billion annually.
Pakistan’s economy, sustained by remittances, external borrowing, real estate speculation, and import-led consumption rather than exports, demands sophisticated leadership, not a bureaucratic placeholder chosen for compliance.
Article 63(1)(c) bars dual nationals from parliament since an elected official answers to voters as the sole political principal, and a second citizenship competes with that loyalty. A central bank governor is not elected, but appointed, and constrained by statute, audit, parliamentary review, and a monetary policy committee, an accountability built on expertise, not a mandate. That is why dual nationality has long been lawful for the wider civil service, precisely because competence, not electoral legitimacy, is what those roles select for. A 2025 Senate report counted roughly 2,365 civil servants or their spouses holding dual nationality under that lawful regime. Extending the Article 63 logic to appointed posts applies a rule built for one office to a fundamentally different one.
The government’s 2026 policy, read past the headline, already leans this way: the Civil Servants (Disclosure and Regulation of Foreign Nationality) Rules require employees to disclose foreign citizenship annually, treating concealment, not citizenship itself, as misconduct. It is a disclosure regime, not a blanket bar.
A second passport is often acquired for reasons of economics and convenience, educating children, or freedom to travel, not disloyalty. The genuine concerns — divided loyalty, foreign leverage, capture by a foreign employer — are real, and better addressed by targeted tools than a passport count: disclosure of foreign assets, recusal where a conflict is shown, and cooling-off periods after work for a foreign government or an institution like the IMF. The US Federal Reserve applies this to its officials. It also catches the single-passport holder who has taken money from a foreign government, someone a citizenship test would wave through.
Pakistan need not start from scratch. In 2022, the prime minister notified the ISI as the Special Vetting Agency for public office holders. The mechanism only needs streamlining to run on specific safeguards, not opaque “cleared” or “not cleared” verdicts that strip the federal government’s own statutory appointment authority.
It is time to remove the dual-nationality bar and age restrictions on appointments to the governor, deputy governor, and Monetary Policy Committee positions. Central banking is one of the few institutions where competence, not compliance, should be the only test. The question worth asking of any candidate is not how many passports are in their drawer, but whether their record and enforceable safeguards assure they will act in the country’s interest. A passport count answers none of that. Performance, integrity, and disclosure do.
The writer is the author of The Shady Economics of International Aid, and holds a PhD in economics from the University of Cambridge. He has served as chief economist of the State Bank and senior advisor to the IMF.
Published in Dawn, October 7th, 2026

title: Unlearned lessons
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE talks between the government and the opposition were doomed from the outset, even though the fact that the two sides sat face to face at the negotiating table was a positive sign. The meeting took place under the shadow of the PTI’s threatened long march to Islamabad, while the government brandished the option of governor’s rule in KP. The tension was palpable. The capital was sealed off with containers and the highways were blocked.
Days before the talks, the military leadership warned against any repeat of a May 9-like situation — a clear message to the opposition not to cross the red line. Some opposition leaders, for their part, wanted a negotiated deal to bring down the political temperature. The prolonged discussions suggested a measure of seriousness on both sides, but mutual distrust and brinkmanship blocked any breakthrough.
The two sides gave contrary accounts of why the talks collapsed after a marathon sitting. The government contended that the opposition backed out after agreeing to a final draft; the other side denied this, saying the differences were too wide to bridge. That so-called final draft is not in the public domain, but two major points of difference appear to have defeated the agreement. The PTI insisted on a meeting with Imran Khan, while the government wanted the KP provincial government to give unqualified support to the counterterrorism operation being carried out by the security forces.
While conceding to the opposition’s demand that the former prime minister be allowed to meet his family and his lawyers, as ordered by the Islamabad High Court, and agreeing to implement the Supreme Court order to arrange his medical treatment, the government was not prepared to let PTI leaders meet and consult him before finalising the agreement — a condition it found unacceptable.
The prevailing political instability has provided greater space to the militants.
The real cause of the stalemate, however, was the issue of provincial government support, and taking ownership of a planned counterterrorism military operation in five southern districts, including the merged Fata regions. For the provincial government this was an extremely tricky matter: it had strongly opposed any kinetic operation involving the displacement of the population, and the bitter memories of earlier operations had created intense public opposition to any such action.
A multiparty meeting called by the provincial government early this year — whose participants included provincial legislators belonging to PML-N, PPP and ANP — had unanimously opposed any large-scale military operation. Considering this, it was hard for the PTI to take ownership of a highly unpopular action.
It may be true that the PTI has no clarity over how to combat the menace of terrorism that has swept a large part of the province. Its inaction, often seen as capitulation, has added to the problem. The ill-equipped police and Counter Terrorism Department have been a major target of militants, resulting in a virtual collapse of the administration in the troubled districts. That inaction could also be attributed to the ongoing confrontation between the PTI and the establishment-backed federal government.
Then there is the question of whether we have a coherent, overarching national security policy and counterterrorism strategy to deal with this existential threat. There has rarely been any debate in parliament on internal security policy. It is all left to the security establishment, with hardly any policy input from the civilian leadership.
KP has witnessed a strong resurgence of militancy over the last five years, which has claimed the lives of thousands of civilians and security personnel. Last year saw the highest number of terrorist attacks in the province since 2013, despite claims of successful intelligence operations that killed hundreds of terrorists. The prevailing political instability has provided greater space to the militants, who are now better equipped and better organised, and who have extended their activities to other parts of the province.
Pakistan has blamed Afghanistan’s Taliban regime for providing sanctuaries and aiding the TTP, and each major terrorist attack is now answered by Pakistani strikes across the border. The closure of the border and of trade between the two countries over the past year has directly affected the local population and added to the tension between Peshawar and Islamabad. There is a serious disconnect in the policy the establishment pursues in dealing with terrorism, and the government needs to address those concerns.
There are no two views about the imperatives of a national security policy, but there is also a need to bring all stakeholders on board for an overarching policy that should not rest entirely on kinetic operations. It is important to address the social and economic issues in order to win public support in the affected areas. The widening trust gap between the state and the people, and the politics of confrontation, are the biggest hurdles in combating terrorism.
With little hope of the two sides returning to the negotiating table, the confrontation has now escalated: the PTI has begun its protest march from the southern KP districts. It is apparent that the PTI has changed its strategy of marching directly on Islamabad. Instead, the party now plans to mobilise its supporters in the province and camp close to the capital rather than march into the city. It is the first instance of a chief executive leading a protest that paralyses his own province.
Meanwhile, the federal government is considering removing the PTI government and imposing a state of emergency or governor’s rule in the province. That would be an extremely dangerous move in a province already facing terrorist attacks, rising nationalism and tension on its border. Any such move by a state already fighting a separatist movement in Balochistan and a revolt-like situation in Azad Kashmir would be disastrous. The province is sitting on a powder keg, and the removal from power of an elected government that enjoys an overwhelming majority in the provincial assembly and broad popular support could ignite it in a way the state would struggle to extinguish. We never learn lessons from our own history, and make the same mistake again and again and expect different results.
The writer is an author and journalist.
