title: Pained minds
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IN Pakistan, mental healthcare is wedged between two extremes — a luxury or a stigma. Estimates cited by the federal health minister are grisly: around 24m require psychiatric support in a country where less than one therapist is available for every 500,000 people. The National Mental Health Policy, launched on Thursday, with the government promising to expand mental healthcare through primary and community-based services, is heartening news. The plan provides a common national structure, while making room for provinces, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir to develop responses as per regional requirements. Its priorities include incorporating mental wellness into primary healthcare services, widening community-centric treatment, early detection, rehabilitation, and more. The need for determined implementation of this framework cannot be overstated.
The prevalence of mental despair and the absence of treatment have contributed to the burden of years ‘lived with disability’, and inflicted profound economic damage. In fraught times, anxiety, depression among the young, suicides and substance abuse surge at an alarming rate. Climate change and digital settings further diminish mental health resilience. The stigma associated with this agony has added to the human toll. Pakistan cannot afford to falter now. The policy’s success depends on changing regressive mindsets, and making access and provision of counsellors available at the tertiary level. Meanwhile, general practitioners should be aware of the importance of identifying symptoms so that patients receive timely psychiatric attention. While affordable care is crucial, there must be consequences for those who overmedicate. Mental health disorders keep children out of classrooms and leave adults without opportunities. Experts say women are twice as susceptible to being diagnosed with depression. The cost of mental illness, internalised shame, and looking away is high. Regular and open conversations about mental health remove entrenched fallacies to ensure that sufferers never become footnotes.

title: Artificial state
author: none@none.com (Aqdas Afzal)
content:
A FEW years ago, as the story goes, it was nearly curtains for the philosophy department at Lahore’s iconic Government College. Thankfully, the college relented, perhaps because Allama Iqbal had once studied philosophy there. Other departments haven’t been so lucky in the wider English-speaking world, where many have faced cuts or closure. In this age of speed, money and results, philosophy appears impractical. If your car breaks down, Socrates won’t fix it. Predictably, college students — and their parents — see philosophy as irrelevant, especially as it lacks ‘scope’ or employability. 
Ironically, philosophers are suddenly in high demand at leading AI firms. This isn’t because techies desire to answer humanity’s big questions. Rather, Silicon Valley’s newfound penchant for philosophers has ominous, if not sinister, motives. AI firms are racing to develop artificial superintelligence — AI that vastly exceeds human capabilities in all domains. To that end, philosophers now help AI firms ponder metaphysical questions: does AI have character, and if not, how can it be developed? Do chatbots like Anthropic’s Claude suffer or can they be harmed?
At this breakneck speed, a superintelligent model may not be far off. Experts are already alarmed at how unpredictable today’s AI can be. In July, OpenAI disclosed that hundreds of its AI agents unexpectedly communicated and banded together to hack Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. No engineer had told them to do it.
To exceed humans, AI firms must first grapple with what it means to have a mind, emotions, and biology. Unsurprisingly, their language now hints that AI has all three. The field of ‘AI interpretability’ focuses on LLMs’ ‘internal reasoning’ and ‘introspection’. Some scholars have even speculated about finding discernible states within LLMs that mirror joy, satisfaction, fear and grief. AI firms also regularly use biological terms like ‘neurons’, ‘training’, and ‘neural networks’ in relation to LLMs.
Granting ‘legal personhood’ to AI will create a moral hazard.
In 1980, the philosopher John Searle imagined a man who does not speak Chinese, locked in a room, matching Chinese symbols to instructions written in English. To an outsider, his replies resemble fluent conversation, but the man understands nothing. A computer, argued Searle, does the same. It manipulates symbols without grasping the meaning. Today, AI firms have revived the very vocabulary Searle warned against.
If AI firms convince the public that AI possesses human traits, it is a short leap to pitching AI as a legal person having the same rights as humans. This is all sci-fi, you say?
All 50 US states treat corporations as legal persons, able to carry out business, including rights to own property, sue, and enter into contracts. Corporations also enjoy constitutional rights. In 2010, in ‘Citizens United vs Federal Election Com­mission’, the US supreme court allowed corporations to spend freely on politics. This steady expansion of corporate rights may become a blueprint for AI personhood.
Granting ‘legal personhood’ to AI will create what economists call a moral hazard, insulating AI progenitors from liability, thereby encouraging even more shortcuts on safety. AI is already on the verge of going rogue, but with legal person status, it could become an actual existential threat to humanity. The gravest threat may be what historian Jill Lepore calls the ‘artificial state’, where power shifts from elected government to machines, algorithms and the corporations that own them. In such a system, citizens delegate to polit­i­c­i­ans, politic­i­ans to bureaucr­ats, bur­eaucrats to contractors, and contractors to AI models — in short, a long delegation cha­in, where decisions are made by AI models nobody voted for. 
Even before AI, Pakistan offers a preview of this delegation problem. Most remedies for its ‘broken’ political system involve carving its provinces into sub-units. Thankfully, a few have also focused on improving the quality of democracy at the local level — making cities politically and financially independent. We should dread the day an AI firm is tasked with fixing Pakistan’s political system.
In the final analysis, AI needs close monitoring. AI regulation isn’t just so-called wokeism. It is a survival imperative. With smart regulation, the path to the artificial state can be blocked. We must also question the idea of AI having a mind, emotions and biology before AI is granted personhood. Perhaps we should re-read Searle, who argued that a computer running a programme can never truly ‘understand’ anything, no matter how convincingly it appears to do so. 
The writercompleted his doctorate in economics on a Fulbright scholarship.

title: IWT’s future
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
TOGETHER with the Kashmir dispute, India’s unilateral suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty has become the biggest source of bilateral friction in the subcontinent.
In a controversial move, New Delhi held the decades-old agreement ‘in abeyance’ in 2025 after the Pahalgam episode. But as Pakistan’s senior leadership has highlighted, Indian brinkmanship in this regard may set a negative precedent globally, while also planting the seeds of a new conflict in South Asia.
    
Speaking at an event in Islamabad the other day, Information Minister Atta Tarar said that India’s unilateral action vis-à-vis the IWT could threaten global water governance. He termed New Delhi’s moves “morally bankrupt and devoid of ethics”.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had raised the issue earlier, when he addressed the UN General Assembly last week. He did not mince his words when he said that diverting Pakistan’s water would amount to an “act of war”.
    
This is not mere rhetoric. The Indus and its tributaries are Pakistan’s lifeline, and the country cannot allow India to blackmail it using these precious waters. India has ruled out restoring the treaty until Pakistan acts against ‘cross-border terrorism’. This is a weak alibi being deployed to take what belongs to Pakistan. New Delhi has remained adamant despite the ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in August that the IWT could not be unilaterally suspended.
India has brushed aside the court’s decision. Along with the key issue of water rights, the larger question is what sort of precedent India wants to set. Its leaders speak of multilateralism and the global ‘rules-based order’.
Yet in practice, when they scupper bilateral treaties and refuse to recognise decisions by respected arbitrators, the Indians in fact promote the law of the jungle. Pakistan must continue to pursue its legitimate rights with regard to the Indus waters. It must also point out the double standards India adheres to — claiming to uphold global norms, yet trampling on international law.
If the IWT dispute is left to fester, or worse, if India takes further steps to cut off Pakistan’s share of water, a new conflict in South Asia is quite possible. In order to avoid such a grim scenario, saner elements in India must work towards restoring the IWT, and addressing all other outstanding issues in a civilised manner.

title: The Pinky paradox
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
ON Sept 26, alleged drug dealer Anmol alias Pinky and her alleged accomplice Sameer were indicted in a narcotics case registered in 2021. This followed Pinky’s acquittal in three other narcotics cases over the summer. She remains in jail, facing several other cases.
Ever since she was arrested in May of this year, Pinky’s case has garnered a ton of media attention; purported voice recordings in which she taunts police over their inability to catch her, and the branding on her alleged product, ‘Queen Medam Pinky’ and ‘Naam hi kafi hai’, have all the ingredients of a gangster movie. Except, of course, that there is a ‘godmother’ at the centre of it all.
What then to make of a woman who appears to have made a name for herself in the male dominated gangster world? As a weekly columnist for over a decade, I’ve written regularly about Pakistani women.
    
I’ve written about innumerable cases in which women are beaten down by the system, by men, by in-laws, by their own male relatives, by the economy and by all the forces that coalesce to keep women ‘in their place’. Often, these columns are obituaries. Just two weeks ago, for instance, I wrote about a nine-year-old girl from Swat named Ishmal, whose only mistake was to go to her neighbour’s house as she often did. She was allegedly sexually assaulted and killed. Or let’s remember Hina Javed’s case from just over a month ago — a woman married to a former professor at Nust, who was found dead in a bathroom after allegedly suffering abuse and torture.
These are the usual stories of women in Pakistan, and I know you know many more than the ones I have written about. Women trapped in abusive and even torturous marriages because they do not know if they will be able to make it on their own. Or women who have tried to make it on their own and are punished at every turn, landlords rejecting them for not having a man of the house, bosses harassing them because they are seen as available because of their single status. And these are stories of the middle class; poverty exacerbates all of these cruelties even further. Life in Pakistan in 2026 is harsh and Hobbesian for everyone, but for women it is a particular kind of hell.
Defiance alone is not a virtue.
Then there is Pinky — an alleged cocaine dealer whose lethal product was packaged under her name. Born into a family of modest means with a home in Lyari’s Baloch Para, she finished Class VIII. According to investigators, she then left for Lahore to pursue modelling. According to police, it was from her former husband, a lawyer and alleged drug dealer, that she learned the drug trade.
Investigators allege that she went on to manage an extensive cocaine network spanning Karachi and Lahore, using riders, social media, benami accounts, and other intermediaries. She allegedly sold to customers in Karachi’s affluent areas. Her story is unusual, but the allegations against her are serious: drug trafficking is not an act of female emancipation simply because the person accused of running the operation is a woman.
Selling drugs is a reprehensible trade. Sadly, many turn to it to escape penury. It is an aspect to reflect on — without turning Pinky’s alleged criminal enterprise into a heroic rebellion. The same poverty and absence of opportunity that can make criminal networks attractive also produce countless victims of the narcotics trade.
Pinky must pay for her crimes. Even as I say that, I cannot help but wonder how many of the wealthy and influential people allegedly connected to her network will face similar scrutiny. Police said an initial forensic examination of her phone identified hundreds of contacts, including 300 alleged active customers, as well as multiple bank accounts allegedly used for payments. Will we ever know who among the powerful benefited from or sustained this trade?
Pakistani society is often eager to make a woman pay even as it looks askance at the sins of male leaders, politicians, industrialists, and others with power. But equality cannot mean transforming an alleged drug dealer into a feminist heroine. It must mean equal accountability: for Pinky if the charges against her are proved, for those who allegedly enabled her operation, and for the wealthy customers whose money made such a lucrative trade possible.
A defiant woman is a rare creature in Pakistan, and one who manages to stay alive while challenging powerful structures may be rarer still. But defiance alone is not a virtue. Pinky’s story may tell us much about gender, poverty, power and hypocrisy in Pakistan. None of that requires us to turn her into a heroine.
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

title: Talks, at last
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
YESTERDAY, the government and opposition finally sat across from each other and talked. A government-led coalition, including representatives of the PPP, and the PTI-led opposition, concluded a round of talks on Friday at the chambers of the National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq in Islamabad.
The meeting had been called after the president and prime minister met on Thursday to discuss the national political and security situation. It seemed like a last-ditch attempt at defusing the escalating political crisis ahead of the PTI’s planned march on the federal capital, scheduled for this Sunday.
    
Another round of talks will be held today, with time running out. Neither side had much to say regarding what was accomplished in the first round. Mr Sadiq’s assertion that parliament is the right forum for talks is correct, but the opposition is equally justified in demanding that the government demonstrate its seriousness. There is a trust deficit that needs to be bridged quickly.
The government’s constant threats to suspend KP’s elected dispensation over a political protest have escalated hostilities considerably. In that context, both sides did well to start talking.
The PTI’s Barrister Gohar Khan called the one-hour meeting “cordial”, which gives hope. The prime minister’s special assistant on political affairs did not share as positive an assessment, however — pointing to the fact that no decisions were taken and there was no clear progress.
The PTI also seems determined to keep its protest call intact during the negotiations, while the government wants it cancelled unconditionally. The opposition has already shown flexibility by delaying the march from Sept 27 to Oct 4 — perhaps it can be convinced to consider another extension to give the talks a proper chance.
It was not a good omen that the opposition leader in the National Assembly boycotted the sit-down. The fact that the PTI went ahead without him shows that it is putting at least some faith in the process.
Opposition leaders said they need to consult former prime minister Imran Khan to finalise their agenda. Permitting a meeting with him at Adiala is an easy, low-cost goodwill gesture for the government and could create a quick breakthrough.
The other important items for the PTI are allowing the jailed leader to be moved to hospital and the release of his sisters who were arrested ahead of the planned march. Taking these steps would help ease tensions.
The point made by PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari regarding unity against terrorism and hostility from neighbours is a fair one, but national unity alone cannot be a reason to shut down legitimate political dissent. Both sides must step back from ultimatums. The threat of governor’s rule must be taken off the table, and the PTI should drop its ‘we will march no matter what’ stance.

title: ‘China model’ fallacies
author: none@none.com (Shahid Mehmood)
content:
ECONOMIC discourse in this country, especi­al­­ly with folks in governance circles, can throw up some very interesting — as well as disturbing — insights. A recent conversation brought up the int­e­­resting case of a preference for the ‘China model’.
What is their conception of this model? Briefly, the belief is in an all-powerful centre that forces its economic commands through long-term plans across the entire country, whips up economic growth through major government interventions, and leaves a limited role for the lower tiers (local) of governance. It is worth contemplating whether these views align with ground realities.
A good place to start is the recent paper by Fengming Lu and Xiao Ma, ‘The rise of China’s electric vehicle industry’, which helps demolish several myths. Champion EV firms like BYD and NIO are all private firms that did not get a single penny in state grants, which, instead, went to SOEs for EV research. Even more astonishing, these firms rose in cities the state apparatus did not identify for EV cluster development. How, then, did these firms accomplish this feat? The short answer: mayors of the cities that were left out teamed up with entrepreneurs, helping them usher in the latest achievement of China’s stellar development story.
Notice that city mayors have the authority to act as they please within their locality. In this case, their initiative and actions undermined the SOEs. Yet, the central government never intervened to prevent it, thus demolishing the myth of an all-powerful centre that micromanages everything and does not tolerate local authority.
The Chinese state mainly acts as a facilitator for development in any way it can. In Pakistan, it’s the opposite.
China has a highly competitive and well-established local tier system. Passage to the higher echelons of the central party is possible only through performance at this level. Unlike in Pakistan, there is no chance of attaining a prominent party position merely by being a scion or progeny of a party head. (Interested readers can look up President Xi Jinping’s road to the presidency.)
Second, it demonstrates that the state is willing to tolerate ‘creative destruction’, a term coined by economist Joseph Schumpeter, to describe how competition and creativity can render some businesses useless. This is classic capitalism, not socialism or communism. In the race for EVs, private competitors left state-run SOEs far behind, but the centre never intervened to prevent their slide. In fact, competition is so intense that it has led to price wars, with some firms expected to fail (one county reportedly lost 6.6 billion yuan on a carmaker it supported).
Similar misconceptions exist around its long-term plans. These actually contain insights of tremendous depth, coming from top-tier experts. Plans are contemplated and debated at length rather than rushed through. The economic debates preceding the 14th party congress offer an apt illustration. In the wake of the Soviet Union’s collapse, between October and December 1991 (known as ‘eleven half-days’), the debate centred on why the USSR’s economy collapsed and what could be done to prevent the same from happening to China.
The end result was the adoption of the famous ‘modern enterprise system’, approved by the party in November 1993, which enunciated “clear property rights, clearly defined rights and responsibilities, separation of government and enterprise, and scientific management”, that would prove to be a critical moment in China’s march to prosperity.
The gist is that prevailing conceptions of China as a centrally administered economy with a benevolent dictator at the helm directing its stellar rise are misplaced. In fact, it is arguably the most decentralised governance system in the world, with more than 80 per cent of public expenditure at the local level, and mayors who enjoy independence in their fiscal and administrative decision-making.
The centre is still very powerful, but not in a manner that we understand. It has some red lines that it enforces. The rich, for example, are not allowed to attain influence to an extent that they are in a position to manipulate the state apparatus by tailoring it in their favour to the detriment of the country and its people. This explains, for example, why Communist Party members are banned from holding golf club memberships.
The underlying philosophy is simple: facilitate capital creation and growth, but prevent it from working against the public good and the country. The state mainly acts as a facilitator for development in any way it can. In Pakistan, it’s the complete opposite. Big capital dictates and manipulates policies, whether through tax exemptions or trillions doled out in public-sector contracts. The sugar mafia is a pertinent example, whose powerful members, sitting in the legislature, sway policies and regulations in their favour. (Note: the above should not be taken as advocacy for anti-capital formation policies. Instead, it should be viewed in terms of regulating capital’s negative spillovers.)
And lest we forget, the corrupt in China are handed the death penalty. Try naming a few cases in Pakistan where a similar predicament befell the corrupt. In essence, China’s remarkable transformation to where it stands today constitutes a long, arduous, and messy process that began with Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms, with the above merely offering a glimpse of that long journey.
Why then clamour for this ‘model’ that no one in our power halls would be willing to implement? After all, that would be hara-kiri for a corrupt, compromised elite which thrives on central control and illegally accrued rents via this system.
Well, more than four years into the current experiment, the economy is still struggling to get out of the stagflationary rut in which it has been stuck since 2022; the average GDP growth has barely surpassed population growth, and all the ‘game changers’ (SIFC, $6 trillion mineral wealth, corporate farming, crypto, and geopolitical rents) have fizzled out. Expectedly, in comes yet another game changer — the ‘China model’.
I cannot speak for others, but if it were up to me, I’d start implementing this model tomorrow. I assume, though, that once the enthusiastic folks in power circles come to grips with what it really implies, they’ll discard it immediately.
The writer is an economist. His current research focuses on long-term analyses of the various issues plaguing Pakistan’s economy, economic reforms and the history of economic thought.

title: Politics of agitation
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
SEPTEMBER emerged as a politically charged month. The PTI and Jamaat-i-Islami announced their plans for long marches on Islamabad. The simultaneous mobilisation by the two parties had raised concerns about potentially prolonged street protests and disruptions in the capital. However, both parties postponed their marches (although the PTI has indicated it would begin its protest over the weekend), which temporarily eased the immediate concern of large-scale agitation. But, despite the postponements, the episode has once again highlighted the recurring pattern of opposition parties resorting to street agitation. It has raised several questions regarding the rationale of this politics of agitation.
Why do some political parties in Pakistan consistently resort to street agitation, road blockades, and prolonged sit-ins, while others continue to place their faith in parliamentary procedures and institutional mechanisms? What does this divergence reveal about the country’s political cultu­re? These questions lie at the heart of understanding the recurring cycle of protests that has come to define much of Pakistan’s contemporary politics.
In Pakistan’s political culture, agitation has recently served as a potent instrument for opposition parties to convert street power into tangible political gains through the ballot box. By orchestrating prolonged protests and sit-ins, parties have succeeded in mobilising their grassroots workers, reinvigorating cadre loyalty, and projecting an im­­­age of resistance against the status quo. Ex­­ces­sive media coverage provides publicity that often elevates relatively smaller actors to the level of na­­tional relevance, while the narrative of standing up for the ‘common man’ against an unresponsive system helps cultivate a saviour-like persona.
This dynamic was most visibly demonstrated by the PTI, whose 2014 Islamabad dharna and 2016 ‘lockdown’ agitation not only kept the party in the headlines for months but also laid the organisational and perceptual groundwork for its dramatic electoral expansion in 2018. Through this strategy, the PTI secured phenomenal electoral gains, from a modest 34 National Assembly seats in 2013 to 120 seats in 2018.
Since 2012, the state’s response to political agitation has undergone a noticeable evolution.
Similar patterns are evident at the regional levels. The TLP registered itself as a political party in 2016 and after its long march on Islamabad in November 2017, it remarkably secured 2.2 million votes in the 2018 elections. Maulana Hidayatur Rehman’s sustained agitation in Gwadar transformed him from a marginal local political figure into a formidable voice of Gwadar, while Hafiz Naeemur Rehman’s high-visibility protests in Karachi have allowed the Jamaat-i-Islami to reclaim political space in urban Sindh. It is precisely this proven formula of converting agitation into both visibility and voter sympathy that appears to have encouraged the current Jamaat chief to attempt replicating the strategy on a national scale.
At its core, however, the recurring resort to agitation also reflects a deep lack of trust in the government, legitimacy of the electoral system, and the taxation system, compounded by the widespread perception of corruption. When citizens believe that taxes are routinely misappropriated rather than spent on public welfare, protests become the default language of political expression, as institutional channels are viewed as ineffective or compromised.
However, this strategy of political agitation also carries significant socioeconomic costs. Prolonged protests and road blockades not only disrupt daily economic activities, they also impose heavy financial burdens on businesses, trade, and ordinary citizens. The PTI’s 2014 Islamabad sit-ins, which stretched for 126 days, and the subsequent waves of agitation in later years, created extended periods of uncertainty, including around 152 days of political and economic instability within a span of two years. As per a recent statement by the finance minister, every single day of protest may inflict an economic loss of around Rs120 billion on Pakistan’s economy. When this figure is applied to the 152 days of protests witnessed over the past decade, the cumulative financial damage is staggering and exposes the severe economic cost of sustained political agitation. These disruptions led to substantial losses in the trade, transport, and retail sectors, while simultaneously damaging market sentiment and eroding investor confidence, as prolonged street unrest signals political instability and policy unpredictability.
Since 2012, the state’s response to political agitation has undergone a noticeable evolution. In the earlier phase, the government largely avoided direct confrontation. Instead, it opted for dialogue and negotiation. Federal ministers were frequently nominated by the prime minister of the time to engage with protest leaders, as seen during Tahirul Qadri’s 2012-13 sit-ins in Islamabad, the PTI’s prolonged 2014 dharna, and the TLP’s 2017 long march. These episodes reflected the government’s preference for political management over force. From 2012 to 2017, the state apparatus largely attempted to defuse tensions through concessions or mediated settlements rather than immediate crackdowns.
Over time, however, this approach has shifted towards greater repression. Successive governments have increasingly relied on heavy-handed tactics, including the use of force, communication blackout, mass arrests, and restrictions on movement to disperse protests. While this strategy has, to some extent, discouraged repeated large-scale national-level agitations by raising the cost of mobilisation, it has simultaneously deepened public resentment towards state institutions. The perception of an increasingly authoritarian response has further eroded public trust in the system, and reinforced the very sense of institutional alienation that often fuels street protests in the first place.
Although both the Jamaat and PTI postponed their long marches to Islamabad, the underlying tension between the opposition’s inclination towards street agitation and the government’s readiness to suppress such mobilisations remains. This recurring pattern continues to raise important questions: Can Pakistan continue to afford the repeated economic and institutional costs of agitation and repression? Or will the state and political actors eventually recognise the need to strengthen formal institutions such as the judiciary, parliament, and the standing committees of the National Assembly and Senate so that grievances can be resolved through dialogue and established democratic mechanisms rather than through the streets?
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: Exit from Iraq
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AMERICAN and British troops have once again shipped out of Iraq. On Wednesday, the foreign forces left the Arab country as per an agreement with the Iraqi government in 2024 that called for wrapping up their decade-old mission against the self-styled Islamic State group. While this deployment was requested by the Iraqis, the Americans and their allies had earlier arrived uninvited, invading Iraq in 2003 to topple its strongman Saddam Hussein. That misadventure had left Iraq in ruins, torn apart by sectarian civil war and a terrorist onslaught by IS. On Wednesday, there was great joy on the streets of Baghdad, indicating that many Iraqis were happy to see the foreign forces go home. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi termed it “a new phase” and declared that Oct 1 would be observed as ‘Sovereignty Day’ every year. Long after IS had been mostly neutralised, the US military presence in Iraq had actually become a liability, with American bases attacked by both Iran and the pro-Tehran Hashd as-Shaabi militias. US President Donald Trump welcomed the latest withdrawal as a “victory”. However, though justifying the need to bring his troops home from Iraq, Mr Trump has gotten stuck in a quagmire because of his war with Iran.
The fact is that American military bases in the Middle East offer only an illusion of security. In reality, they have been a source of instability. Not only have these facilities been used to destabilise and occupy regional states — Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, etc — they also put targets on the countries that host them. The fantasy of the American security umbrella was very quickly shattered for the Gulf states when Iranian missiles targeted them, as Tehran claimed that the attacks against it were launched from these US bases. Following the example of its departure from Iraq, the US must further reduce its military footprint in the Middle East. It is by no means a global policeman, and its military forays have only resulted in chaos in the region. Instead, the people of the region — the Arabs, Iranians, Turks, and other nations — should be able to work out a mutual security structure based on non-aggression. The age of empire and Cold War calculations is over. Sovereign states of the Middle East can decide their fate for themselves, and do not need powerful external patrons to ‘protect’ them.

title: Lahore’s ozone warning
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
LAHORE has received another warning that its air pollution crisis cannot be treated as a problem that begins with winter smog. A new assessment by the EU’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service places the city among those with “extremely poor” ground-level ozone levels. Unlike the protective ozone layer high in the atmosphere, ground-level ozone is a harmful pollutant formed when sunlight and heat act on emissions from vehicles, industry and other sources. The finding is especially troubling because rising temperatures can intensify its formation. Lahore is, therefore, confronting a year-round interaction between dirty air, urban emissions and climate change. Globally, almost 40pc of the population was exposed to extremely high ozone levels this year, according to CAMS. Asia fared even worse, with about 60pc of its population facing such exposure.
Punjab deserves credit for acting earlier this year. Its pre-smog crackdown on construction dust, waste and crop burning, brick kilns and vehicle emissions was a welcome shift from reactive governance. But the latest assessment reinforces the point made then: temporary drives will not be enough. Ozone cannot be reduced by targeting dust alone. The government must cut the precursor gases that create it, particularly nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds. That means rigorous vehicle emissions testing, cleaner fuels, stronger industrial controls, reliable public transport and enforcement against open burning. Lahore also needs continuous monitoring that separately tracks ozone, particulate matter and other pollutants, with readings and enforcement data made public. Agricultural residue management must be supported with affordable alternatives to burning, while industries and kilns should face sustained compliance checks. Urban planning, traffic policy and energy use must also be treated as air quality policy. The province must recognise that Lahore’s pollution emergency does not end when the winter haze lifts. Clean air requires permanent policy, transparent enforcement and measurable reductions in emissions.

title: Afghan irredentism
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
PAKISTAN’S relations with Afghanistan have remained hostage to Afghan irredentism, which is a consequence of deep-seated historical animosities. The antipathy towards Pakistan was engendered through a false sense of entitlement about areas of Pakistan that in the past had once supposedly been part of Afghanistan. Generations in Afghanistan have been reared on a distorted version of history that regards the Pak-Afghan border as a historical injustice.
Little do these irredentists know that goi­ng by that logic Afghanistan has remained part of the Maurya and Mughal empires, while Sikhs, under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, had advanced up to Peshawar in 1834. Sub­sequently, the British and Afghans kept sparring over territories across British India and the Afghan frontier, resulting in three Anglo-Afghan wars.
The frontier between British India and Afghanistan was formalised in 1893 throu­­gh the Durand Line Agreement between Emir Abdur Rahman of Afghanistan and Sir Hen­ry Mortimer Durand, foreign secretary of British India. In fact, it was Emir Abdur Rah­­man who wanted to formalise Afghan­istan’s borders both with Russia and British India.
Abdur Rahman requested the British In­­dian government to delineate the border bet­­ween the two states. He specifically req­uested Mortimer Durand to lead the mission. Following the agreement, joint commissions demarcated the border over several years and thereafter, several treaties were concluded. Each reaffirmed both parties’ commitments to respecting the boundary.
Afghan irredentism has kept emerging with regularity.
During the course of demarcation, Afghanistan gained territory not only from British India but also from Russia and Iran.
As a legatee state of British India, Pakis­tan inherited the border agreement as per the customary international law principle of uti possidetis juris (new states inherit pre-existing borders). However, Afghanistan’s representative cast the sole dissenting vote against Pakistan’s inclusion in the UN. Tho­ugh that negative vote was removed after a few weeks, the bad blood of Afghan irredentism continued to plague bilateral ties.
A Loya Jirga declared all previous agreements regarding the international boundary invalid in July 1949, followed by border skirmishes and diplomatic stand-offs. Afghan forces entered Pakistani territory and were repelled after six days. Afghanistan kept providing political and financial support to Pakhtunistan-oriented elements in the 1950s while Afghan prime minister Mohammad Daoud condemned Pakistan’s One Unit arrangement, promising Afghan government support to Pakhtuns in Pakistan. Afghan mobs violated Pakistan’s diplomatic missions at Kabul, Jalalabad and Kandahar.
Afghan troops in disguise, along with anti-Pakistan tribesmen, entered Bajaur in September 1960 under the direction of prime minister Daoud. Local tribesmen and Frontier Corps scouts initially resisted their advance while regular Pakistani forces, including air force and artillery, beat back Afghan troops, souring relations till 1963.
After the deposition of King Zahir Shah by Daoud in 1973, Afghan intervention in Pakistan became more brazen. Afghanistan openly supported pro-Pakhtunistan elements. Afghanistan under Sardar Daoud also remained a veritable support base for the Baloch insurgency. Despite maximum support to Afghans in their freedom struggle during the Soviet invasion (1979-89), Afghan irredentism kept emerging with metronomic regularity, irrespective of the regime in power.
From 1996 to 2001, Taliban-controlled Af­­ghanistan kept harbouring terrorist org­a­n­i­s­­ations including Al Qaeda, ETIM, and IMU. These groups influenced Pakistan’s ex-Fata region as well. The armed groups based in Afghan territory kept conducting cross-border at­­tacks against Pakis­­­tan from 2002 to 2006, encouraging the rise of terrorist entities like TTP. When Pak­istan fin­ally started fencing its border in 2017, Afghan troops targeted Pakistani forces at Torkham, repeating similar actions at Parachinar, Chaman, Bajaur and Chitral.
Pakistan had welcomed the Taliban regime after the 2021 US withdrawal in good neighbourly spirit, offering humanitarian and economic support at a time when most of the world was treating it as a pariah regime. The Taliban regime in turn gave impetus to anti-Pakistan terrorists like the TTP holed up in Afghanistan. In 2021, terrorist incidents saw a 42 per cent rise, owing to the Afghan Taliban’s takeover of Kabul and the subsequent release of hardened militants from various Afghan jails. From 128 terrorist incidents in 2021 to over 1,200 in 2025, there has been a steady rise in Taliban-regime enabled terrorist violence in Pakistan.
Despite continued positive engagement by Pakistan, the Taliban regime has displayed obduracy and non-cooperation on the counterterrorism front by using terrorism as a low-cost option for leverage.
The writer holds a PhD from Nust.

title: Fragile cryosphere
author: none@none.com (Naseer Memon)
content:
IN contrast to last year’s catastrophic floods, this year’s monsoon flows drained through the plains of Pakistan without wreaking a major disaster. Nonetheless, the highlands of Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral did not remain unaffected.
Not too far away, Nepal experienced a horrific disaster in August. The Himalayan nation endured one of its worst catastrophes when a huge mass of glacial ice and rock collapsed down a slope in the Himalayas near the Langtang region. Within half an hour, it caused an unprecedented surge — as high as nine metres — in the Bhote Koshi/Trishuli river system. Over 1,400 people died. Thousands more went missing. A month later, a massive section of the mountainside collapsed into the swollen Kali Gandaki River after days of heavy rain, sending enormous quantities of soil, rock and debris into the water. This wave of floods and landslides caused at least two dozen deaths.
Pakistan, China, India, Nepal, and Bhutan lie along the axis of disaster — the Hindu Kush-Himalaya (HKH) mountain system, also referred to as the ‘Third Pole’ because of its massive concentration of ice and glaciers. These water towers of Asia feed 10 major river systems and support the livelihoods of over two billion people in the region. Ironically, these mountains also spawn hydro-climatic disasters in the region. This explains the vulnerability of Pakistan’s highlands, as the Indus and other rivers flowing into the country draw water from these majestic mountains. The Nepal tra­gedy should be viewed as an early war­­ning for Pakistan, especially for areas located in the highly fragile Hindu Kush, Karakoram and western Himal­ayan region. The phenomenon bears a stark resemblance to the relatively smaller-scale flash floods that occur almost yearly in the mountains of GB and KP.
In its August 2026 update, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission warned that it had identified 131 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, most of them in GB and KP. The number of unfrozen PDGLs rose from 40 to 105 within a month due to higher temperatures. These findings reinforce the ominous report of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Its assessment of the HKH region identified 25,614 glacial lakes across major river basins. The report also highlighted the risks linked to moraine-dammed lakes near retreating glaciers.
The Nepal tragedy should be seen as a warning for Pakistan.
These manifestations cannot be solely attributed to climate change, as human intervention is aggravating the impact of natural processes. The cryosphere’s health depends on several factors, including forests, vegetation, and soil stability. As forests vanish, hilly slopes are exposed and the runoff from rainwater and glacial melt increases. Flash floods become more violent and tend to carry larger amounts of debris.
A study supported by the ICIMOD revealed that approximately 9,288 acres of forest were lost in Chitral between 1992 and 2009. The annual rate of deforestation accelerated from 0.14 per cent in 1992-2000 to 0.54pc in 2000-2009. Deforestation is an equally alarming trend in GB, where the forest cover has declined to 615,798 acres, comprising only 3.57pc of the total area.
Population growth compounds environmental pressures. GB’s population was listed at around 881,000 in the 1998 census. By 2023, it had increased to some 1.5 million people. Similarly, Chitral recorded a population of about 516,000 in 2023. Demographic pressure amid weak land regulation has led to unregulated settlements in the dry beds of flood nullahs. A growing population increa­ses the demand for land, which is sca­rce on mountain terraces and in narrow valleys. Dry nullahs are often mistaken for wasteland and used to build houses, which eventually collapse under the wrath of unforeseen gushing floods.
In July 2026, Suparco highlighted the serious challenge of relentless settlement expansion along a natural glacial lake-fed stream near Gilgit city. Satellite imagery comparing construction in 2023 to that of a decade earlier indicated the rapid expansion of settlements along this natural stream. Suparco is alarmed that the narrowed channels may not safely carry high flows.
The Nepal tragedy needs careful analysis to understand the parallels with the vulnerability of our cryosphere. Disaster managers should treat the catastrophe as an early warning. Residential and commercial development along mountain riverbanks, as well as deforestation in the watershed, should be strictly prohibited to avert human tragedy.
The writer is a senior adviser on water governance at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.
naseer_memon@sdpi.org
Published in Dawn, October 1st, 2026

title: Refinery upgradation plans
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
AFTER a full year of criticism that while it had stabilised the economy it had offered no vision for reform, the government is finally moving. A string of recent announcements makes the reform path clearer. Refineries are being asked to upgrade their operations in return for concessions granted in the Brownfield Refinery Upgradation Policy. A number of power distribution companies are being prepared for privatisation, and the ministry has announced the beginning of power wheeling, an important reform stuck in limbo since 2017 and an essential plank in any effort to reform power pricing.
The finance ministry is helping arrange resources for the refineries and the newly privatised PIA, as well as moving along the commitments for the Reko Diq project. A meeting between the finance minister and officials from the US Exim Bank was wrongly interpreted by many as an effort by the government to borrow on behalf of the newly privatised PIA for aircraft procurement. It turned out to be nothing of the sort. Meanwhile, March saw a spectrum auction, setting the stage for the rollout of 5G telecommunications in Pakistan; unlike the last auction in 2021, which saw a lacklustre response, three large telecoms participated and picked up spectrum at a price tag of $500 million.
So things are finally beginning to move on the structural front. Obviously, it is too early to call the results, but if the envisioned changes behind these actions bear fruit, reform momentum can certainly start to build. There are a few things to be mindful of, however.
Consider the refinery upgradation plan. In a recent interaction with journalists and industry leaders, the petroleum minister allowed himself to express some annoyance that Pakistan’s refineries can only handle “the sweetest grades of crude”. This means they are using the most basic technology in their sector. His point was to underline the importance of the upgradation policy, and he emphasised that after the upgrades, Pakistan could also become an exporter of refined products.
If the new rules and policy succeed in getting the refiners to do what they have not done in the past 20 years, that will be a big, positive step.
Fair enough. But of the four refineries that have submitted upgradation plans, only one has the books to bear the cost. That one is Attock Refinery. The other three — National Refinery, Cynergico, and Pakistan Refinery Ltd — will struggle to raise the funds, given their books. Between the four, upgrades worth $4.2 billion have been announced. ARL’s plan is worth $600m and comes to around 1.5 times its (real) equity, which makes the plan realistic. For the others, the figures are seven to 25 times their (real) equity, which leaves one wondering about their financing plans.
ARL could potentially put up 30 per cent of its equity share for the project from its own cash holdings, and the remainder would be 2.9 times its EBITDA, which is manageable. It might also need to support NRL’s financing since it owns a 25pc stake in the latter. But the other refiners will need support from multilateral lenders or an Exim bank to arrange resources for their plans. This was one reason the finance minister met officials from the US Exim Bank: to help arrange the resources the refiners, PIA, and the Reko Diq project will require. As of now, there is no reason to believe that this will create any public liabilities for the country.
The refineries have been given the option to sign up for a ‘Refinery Upgradation Account’ ratified by the cabinet in August. The fund has withdrawal rules, including a requirement that projects be completed within five years, with incentives for early completion, penalties for late completion, and sales tax exemption for upgradation equipment. The rules are meant to prevent a repeat of the alleged misuse of the so-called deemed duty in the Musharraf years — when refiners were given an incentive to build stocks and they allegedly took the incentive but did not build any stock. That episode was documented in the Justice Rana Bhagwandas Judicial Commission report of 2009. This time, the funds raised from the incentives will be maintained in an account operated by the ministry, and the refiners will be able to withdraw only after showing compliance with the terms of use of this fund.
If the new rules and policy succeed in getting the refiners to do what they have not done in the past 20 years, that will be a big, positive step. But much hinges on whether they can raise the financing, given the scale of the projects they have announced.
Likewise, the telcos stepped forward to participate in the 5G spectrum auction after the last auction saw lukewarm participation in 2021. The bids were at or near the reserve price for most bands. Industry’s demand was that they be allowed to pay in rupees, at an exchange rate fixed at the time of the auction, and to stretch their payments over a longer period of time at Kibor plus 3pc. These concessions were granted. In return, they must introduce 5G in Islamabad first, then expand to 10 cities nationwide by 2030, and increase minimum speeds from 20mbps on 4G to 50mbps on 5G. In addition, some telcos have announced investment plans to expand their business base in Pakistan, with Jazz leading the pack through a $1bn investment plan over the next three years.
These are significant steps, including the one we have not been able to discuss — the introduction of wheeling in the power sector. If they go through as envisaged, the impact will be manifest, with greater resilience in our energy supply chain against international shocks, faster communications, and more flexibility in power-provisioning arrangements. Let’s hope for the best, but remain vigilant about the pitfalls as these plans move towards implementation.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Homeward bound
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
FIVE months after Somali pirates captured an oil tanker carrying a 19-member multinational crew, Somali maritime police have recovered the vessel off the coast of Puntland. The Foreign Office has confirmed five casualties — out of the 10 Pakistani seamen, three have died with four wounded during the rescue operation; a total of five sailors lost their lives. Despite efforts — social media videos show hostages asking the Pakistani government to engage with their captors; hapless families staging protests and facing police brutality, and even calling on foreign governments and international agencies to take coordinated action — losses could not be averted. Regrettably, a forceful approach involving collaborative action with Indonesia, India and Sri Lanka was missing on the part of the government. Hence, this homeward journey is bittersweet.
Seajacks by pirate gangs had subsided around the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. But, fuelled by political upheaval, poverty and aid cuts, piracy is back with a vengeance. Recent instances suggest that, due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, this route needs amplified transnational patrolling. Clearly, this year’s tally of over 100 ships struck and 40 hijacked with 15 attacks in April alone confirms that a prime trade passage has become perilous. We cannot lose more time. An international naval cover, comprising satellite information, emergency services, and a tracking dashboard effective in strife-torn waterways for navigational safety, is vital. In short, only a modern maritime protection framework alongside contingency plans can prevent future shocks. Meanwhile, local labour rights bodies must protect sailors from the coercive policies of shipping companies and other patrons. Global trade relies on mariners. They must have the power to choose secure routes without fear of repercussions. Additionally, the government is obligated to provide compensation to affected families and to ensure that no distressed citizen faces official apathy.

title: Fixing bond markets
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE plan to deepen the domestic local currency bond market by allowing the public to trade government securities through the stock market should help address a weakness long concealed by the sovereign’s easy access to bank borrowings. Pakistan’s large government securities market lacks the depth and diversification needed to allow securities to be widely held, actively traded and efficiently priced. Banks, holding about 78pc of government securities with sovereign paper accounting for roughly 62pc of their assets, have therefore little reason to seek ‘riskier’ private borrowers. Consequently, small firms, farmers and potential homebuyers struggle to obtain credit. The proposed reforms recognise this structural weakness. More predictable and market-based issuance, greater secondary-market liquidity, a functioning repo market and a broader investor base are all necessary. Allowing individuals to trade exchange-listed government securities through their banks should also improve access and price discovery. But can the reforms change how the market works?
That requires breaking the banks’ dominance. Pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, retail investors, and eventually, foreign investors must become bigger participants. They need both access and incentives to hold and trade rupee securities. Secondary-market liquidity is equally important. Primary dealers should have incentives to make markets rather than merely participate in government auctions. The proposed review of the primary-dealer framework and securities-lending facility could help. The IMF should push this logic further. The government must borrow less from commercial banks. Reducing bank borrowing would force greater reliance on actual market financing, creating room for banks to lend to productive private activity.
The market should also be broadened beyond government debt. The government could require SOEs to raise at least one-third of all future local currency borrowing through bonds. This would create more issuers, diversify instruments and maturities, and expose SOE borrowing to greater market scrutiny. Demand can be boosted through targeted tax incentives for investors holding local currency bonds issued by SOEs and private companies. Such incentives should encourage longer-term investment. Further, transparently priced government securities across maturities can provide benchmarks against which private companies price their own debt. Over time, this could reduce the economy’s overreliance on bank lending. That said, the government must avoid treating the bond market reform as a way to finance itself more easily. A deeper market should reduce refinancing risks, improve monetary policy transmission and redirect savings to productive investment. The measure of success cannot be the number of bonds issued. It must be who buys them, how actively they trade, how liquid the market becomes and whether businesses have better access to long-term capital.

title: Misunderstanding Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Basil Nabi Malik)
content:
THE foundational basis of Pakistan and the objectives behind the country’s creation remain a subject of debate. One side emphasises religion above all else and argues that the basis for creating Pakistan was Islam itself. On the other hand, some commentators contend that Pakistan was created for the residents of specific regions, the majority of whom were Muslims, so that they could live their lives freely and without subjugation. Although religion was undeniably important, the primary goal was to secure the people’s free will and freedom.
Even without debating which worldview is accurate — if any — we can agree on a few truths. First, Pakistan was born through the will and struggle of its people. Second, the decision to create Pakistan was achieved and affirmed through their votes. And finally, Pakistan was brought into being through a process that can, arguably, be considered democratic.
In essence, the establishment of Pakistan was people-centric. And when the ‘people’ in question share a single culture, language, history, and geography, it becomes easy to categorise them as a monolithic community with a singular identity. However, when a nation comprises diverse ethnic groups with distinct cultures and histories running parallel to one another, neatly situated in separate regions of a land seeking to unite, the mechanics of political representation necessarily change.
Unlike a single monolithic community represented by a unitary voice, multiple distinct communities seeking union often have separate representatives, at least initially, to protect their specific interests within the broader polity. The union is not the merging of a single people, but a voluntary arrangement among distinct communities with shared goals. To achieve this, these communities, through their representatives, discuss, negotiate, and agree on the union’s dynamics, defining which powers are transferred to the central state and which remain local.
Commentators frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself.
This process transfers sovereignty from individual communities to a united entity that becomes greater than the sum of its parts, while protecting regional rights and identities. The goal of such a union is a better shared future; unity is seen as offering greater benefits than division. This fusion of distinct groups into a singular national framework is the essence of entering into a social contract.
Pakistan, which is home to diverse ethnicities and communities, is said to have entered into precisely this type of union right after independence. For many, that social contract was earlier epitomised by the Lahore Resolution of 1940; for others, it was crystallised in the 1973 Constitution. Whichever document one examines, the formal recognition and celebration of diversity are recurring themes.
Pakistan was always intended to be pluralistic, with communities coming together to pool their resources and cede certain freedoms for the collective good. Pakistan came into being for them, not despite them. Abdul Wali Khan articulated well the vision of what Pakistan could be, noting that despite their distinct identities, the federating units were akin to “flowers with their distinct colours and fragrance” that “blend into a bouquet, manifesting their unity in diversity”. Ultimately, the country’s founding idea is rooted in protecting its people, their cultures, languages, and rights. That is what it ought to be, and whether anyone likes it or not, this is what it was always meant to be.
Why is this discussion so critical today? Because when commentators debate whether creating more provinces is necessary for a prosperous Pakistan, whether local governments need to be strengthened, or whether addressing the missing persons issue is key to winning hearts and minds, they frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself. This premise is intrinsically linked to the people’s will and aspirations. As with any major decision, altering provincial boundaries, whether by creating fewer or more provinces or restructuring existing ones, must remain a choice driven directly by the people whose goals are bound to Pakistan’s genesis. Similarly, the people must decide the role of local governments, and the resolution of the missing persons crisis must be as great a priority as the people make it.
If you remove the popular will from this decision-making process, you strike at the core of Pakistan’s founding identity. You not only carve up administrative boundaries and dismiss popularly held convictions, but also dismember the very vision articulated in the 1940 Resolution, codified in the 1973 Constitution, and reaffirmed through the 18th Amendment.
Democracy is neither a luxury that Pakistan cannot afford nor is it a failed concept. If anything, when allowed to function, democratic governance is the single thread that has kept this federation together throughout its turbulent history. It maintains the vital link between the state and the populace that gave it birth. If new administrative units are to be carved out or other consequential decisions to be taken, those decisions belong exclusively to the public, not to self-appointed arbiters who claim to know better than the citizens themselves.
After all, armies did not create Pakistan; the people’s vote did. War tacticians did not envision Pakistan; politicians, lawyers, and civilians did. A war did not lead the nation to independence; a barrister did. Consequently, the bond between the Pakistani state and its citizens is as intrinsic and consequential as water is to fish, instruments are to musicians, and ‘national interest’ is to our armed forces.
If you remove the people from decision-making, you strip away the soul of the country. What remains is merely a land without a people, a people without a voice, and a country without a purpose, with nothing left but despair.
The writer is a lawyer based in Karachi.

title: The privatisation of resilience
author: syed.siddiq.hussain
content:
What happens when powerful people stop believing that the future can be salvaged, and they instead start preparing to survive its destruction?

That is the unsettling question at the heart of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, the new book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. The book argues that a new political formation is emerging from the convergence of religious fundamentalists, ethno-nationalists, Silicon Valley billionaires and other reactionaries. What connects them is not necessarily a common political programme, but an increasingly apocalyptic imagination: the conviction that some catastrophic rupture is coming and that they will somehow be the ones to survive it.

Klein calls this "end-times fascism". Unlike twentieth-century fascism, which sought national rebirth through authoritarianism and exclusion, today's far right increasingly wants to prepare for a world shaped by climate change, resource scarcity, mass migration and other crises.

Klein's ongoing work for more than the last two decades has explored the growing power of corporations, how elites exploit crises for their own benefit, and now how the wealthy seek to insulate themselves from catastrophe.

In a recent interview about the book, she offers a jolting observation about wealth itself: "Wealth has its own deranging effects." Humans, she observes, need stories to make sense of the world around them. The ultra-rich are no different: they, too, need stories to explain why they possess so much while others have so little. The answer can become a story of superiority: that there is something about the wealthy person that justifies their extraordinary share of resources, with the implicit conclusion that inequality is deserved.

This is where Klein's argument becomes particularly relevant to the Global South.

In wealthy countries, apocalyptic politics may take the form of the eccentric fantasy of billionaires to build bunkers or imagine escaping to Mars. In countries such as Pakistan, however, catastrophe is already part of everyday political and economic life. Floods, heatwaves, water insecurity and toxic air are no longer distant possibilities. Yet, the consequences of these emergent threats are not distributed equally. Those who can afford it can protect themselves from the harshest forms of the climate apocalypse.

People with money can purchase safer land, gated housing, private security, generators, solar power, air conditioning, private healthcare and reliable water supplies. They can move away from areas threatened by flooding or extreme heat. They can send their children abroad and, if they have the means, can even build new lives elsewhere.

For poorer citizens, resilience often means trying to navigate weak and apathetic public systems. They remain dependent on increasingly resource constrained public hospitals, schools, water supplies and infrastructure.

Even something as mundane as an air purifier has become a marker of class. In Lahore, where toxic air is a recurring crisis, the air purifier has acquired something of the status once occupied by the UPS during the worst of load-shedding: a private technological solution to a public failure.

The idea of "end-times fascism" can thus be extended beyond the politics of the American far right. In the Global South, it can take the form of a politics of elite insulation: the acceptance that public systems will fail, accompanied by the assumption that those with wealth will somehow be protected.

In Pakistan, where the impacts of the global climate crisis are being acutely felt and the country has limited capacity to contend with these threats, the question becomes: who gets to adapt? If resilience must be purchased, it becomes a privilege.

Climate change is not only making Pakistan more unequal; it is also illustrating how affluence determines who can secure some protection from its effects, making those who can afford it increasingly indifferent to the need to address these public problems.

That is not disaster mitigation. It is the privatisation of resilience.

title: Three revolutions
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
THE past 250 years have seen a tsunami of revolutions — the American, the French, the Chinese, and imitating them, the Cuban. Their waves swept across the world, impacting us today and, as Chairman Mao Zedong predicted, they will affect tomorrow’s history. This year, friends of America celebrate its first 250 years; its detractors see them as its last 250 years. America enjoys the pre-eminence that capitalism promised — at a Faustian price, redeemable in US dollars. America is discomfited by Russia, a perpetual migraine; China, a recurring malaise; and Cuba, an irritating thorn in its side.
A recent book by Simon Hall — Three Revolutions: Russia, China and Cuba (2025) — examines the genesis of their social upheavals. Interestingly, he links them to three writers (all American) who happened to be in the right place at the right time: John Reed, who in 1917 witnessed the ignition of the Russian Revolution; Edgar Snow, who met Mao and those who had survived the gruelling Long March of 1934-35; and Herbert Matthews, a New York Times correspondent, who in 1957 wriggled into Cuba and watched Fidel Castro’s underfunded but determined bid to depose Gen Batista. The three wrote accounts of their experiences and interaction with leaders, especially Lenin, Mao and Fidel Castro. They provided authentic, corrective insights into the social cataclysms that continue to be misunderstood by the West.
In 1917, Reed sees the storming of the czar’s Winter Palace in Petrograd (now St Petersburg). Looters are prevented from despoiling the palace’s treasures and opulent furnishings by “self-appointed sentinels”, who shout: “Comrades! Don’t take anything! This is the property of the people!” Another diligent sailor guarding the Winter Palace refuses entry to a new provisional government minister and the city’s mayor. “What will you do?” the two unarmed civilians ask him. The burly sailor replies: “We will spank you, and if necessary, shoot you!”
On meeting Lenin, Reed notices that he “looks through you with those terrible eyes … of being intensely interested”. Reed’s book Ten Days That Shook the World (1919) quotes Trotsky’s recollection of how Lenin, on Oct 10, 1917, scribbled a call for armed insurrection “hastily … with the gnawed end of a pencil on a sheet of paper from a child’s notebook ruled in squares”.
Internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions.
Lenin’s “sealed train” journey, from Switzerland across Germany and Finland to Russia, was more comfortable than the privations of the Long March. Of the 100,000 troops and party stalwarts who started from Jiangxi, only 6,000 or so reached Yan’an, 9,000 kilometres away. Edgar Snow first met Mao in 1936. He described him as a “gaunt, rather Lincolnesque figure … with a face of intellectual shrewdness”. He attributes Mao’s genius to “his uncanny ability to embody the demands of millions of his fellow citizens — above all, the peasantry”.
Snow converted memories of a three-month stay in China into a book — Red Star over China (1937). It had an immeasurable impact, even in Washington’s highest circles. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s secretary of the interior, H. Ickes, remarked presciently that “any people that can do what the Red Army did during the Long March and after” were “positively invincible”.
Simon Hall’s inclusion of the Cuban revolution of 1956-59 may appear surprising until one reads how Castro achieved it. Arrested by Gen Batista’s soldiers, Castro’s life is spared by a compassionate lieutenant who tells his troops: “Don’t shoot. You can’t kill ideas”. Castro is tried and sentenced to 15 years in jail. In court, he makes a defiant spe­ech: “I do not fear prison[.] Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.”
Batista made the mistake of granting Castro an early am­­nesty. Castro repaid the favour by returning to Cuba from exile in Mexico. In 1956, he landed in Granma — “a creaking, leaking leisure yacht”. It was less “a landing than a shipwreck”. Harassed by Batista’s soldiers, Castro hid in the Sierra Maestra mountains — the commander of “two men, a couple of rifles and 120 rounds of ammunition”. There, he is joined by his brother Raúl, who brought five guns. Castro says, with bravado: “That makes seven. We have won the war!”
Herbert Matthews interviewed Castro in his Sierra hideout, writing afterwards: “He has caught the imagination of the youth of Cuba [because] he is an educated, dedicated fanatic, a man of ideals, of courage, and of remarkable qualities of leadership.” Within three years, Castro toppled the US-supported Gen Batista.
In the 21st century, internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions. Autocracies may blindfold eyes that dare to see. Revolutions, though, like tsunamis, are unpredictable. They do not wait for submissive activists who, in Lenin’s words, sit in “armchair ideas” plotting “armchair action”.
The writer is an author.

The article details key moments and leaders of these revolutions: Lenin's leadership in the Russian Revolution, Mao's genius and the arduous Long March in China, and Fidel Castro's defiant struggle and eventual victory in Cuba.

It concludes by contrasting historical revolutions with 21st-century internecine conflicts but emphasizes the unpredictable and transformative power of genuine uprisings, which do not wait for 'armchair action'.

title: Water shortage
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THAT the country is entering the Rabi season with an anticipated water shortage of nearly 25pc, the lowest carryover since 2021, is a matter of serious concern. It is likely to hit the next wheat harvest hard — a staple food crop already under stress owing to bad policies. Wheat output fell to 27.5 million tonnes against a 29.7m target and 32m consumption last season, requiring imports. Now farmers face less water. The shortage is not simply a consequence of poor rainfall or hydrology. Water management decisions have also contributed to it. According to a report in this paper, more than 1MAF of water that could have been conserved was released from reservoirs during Kharif. Political pressure reportedly played a role in these releases. If so, the episode exposes an entrenched weakness in national water management. The fact that the country continues to manage water driven by short-term political needs instead of long-term planning must change.
The management of reservoirs should follow transparent rules based on water availability, crop requirements, environmental needs and future risks. There is also a need to distinguish between wasteful releases and legitimate environmental flows. Rivers cannot be reduced to irrigation channels. They require water to sustain their ecosystems. Environmental needs must be properly calculated and incorporated into planning. The coming shortage will also revive the old provincial dispute. Irsa will have to distribute a smaller pool of water among the provinces. The existing arrangements already generate disagreement, particularly over how shortages should be shared. Severe shortages will intensify interprovincial tensions — which the centre must prevent. Decisions should be based on verifiable data, in accordance with the Water Apportionment Accord, 1991. The government must also invest in irrigation efficiency and water conservation. Farmers cannot be expected to bear the cost of decades of institutional neglect. The larger failure is that our policymakers still treat water shortages as emergencies rather than as a permanent national constraint. That approach is not sustainable. Climate change makes water availability less predictable while population and food demand continue to rise. The country, therefore, needs a water policy that looks beyond one crop, one harvest and one province. It needs to conserve more, waste less and plan years ahead.
Published in Dawn, September 30th, 2026

The impending shortage is expected to intensify interprovincial water disputes, mandating impartial, data-driven distribution based on the Water Apportionment Accord, 1991, and a shift towards a proactive, long-term national water policy focused on conservation and efficiency.

title: Kashmir unresolved
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
SEVEN years after India revoked occupied Kashmir’s limited autonomy, disquiet continues in the disputed region over the prevailing state of affairs. Even loyalist parties in India’s good books are not happy. This was reflected in a resolution passed by the held region’s assembly on Monday, which called for a restoration of statehood that was scrapped when the Indian constitution’s Article 370 was abrogated in 2019. The occupied area’s chief minister, Omar Abdullah, claimed that statehood was “our right”. BJP lawmakers termed the resolution “anti-national”. Two similar resolutions have been passed over the years by the IHK legislature.
The problem goes far deeper than the restoration of the status quo ante that existed before August 2019. The core issue is the Kashmiris’ right to self-determination, which India has been blocking since the division of the subcontinent. Unless this core issue is addressed with justice, the problem will linger as Kashmiris in the occupied territory are denied their fundamental rights. While speaking at the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also highlighted the Kashmir issue, saying that Kashmiris had been waiting “for eight decades” for the UN to fulfil its commitments. He also pointed out the human rights violations that India has carried out against the Kashmiri population. Turkiye’s President Recep Erdogan, while speaking at the UNGA, similarly called for a resolution of the Kashmir question as per the “relevant resolutions”.
The human rights situation in the disputed region is very grim. A UN report from November 2025 has condemned the arbitrary arrests, suspicious deaths in custody, torture and “discriminatory treatment of Kashmiri and Muslim communities”. Held Kashmir’s wounds cannot be left to fester. The people of Kashmir, including even those politicians who were or are close to New Delhi, are chafing under the post-Article 370 regime in the held region. Along with rights abuses, there is also alarm over the demographic changes in IHK, as the Kashmiris are being turned into a minority in their own land. The just solution lies in India addressing the issue through a trilateral dialogue involving the legitimate representatives of the Kashmiri people and Pakistan. India’s rulers can continue to believe the fiction that occupied Kashmir is an ‘integral’ part of their country. But that does nothing to address the dissatisfaction that both the common Kashmiri and the political elite of the region feel towards Indian rule. The dispute has poisoned all chances of normalisation in South Asia. Instead of arrogantly dismissing talk of freedom, India’s rulers need to listen to voices from IHK, and together with Pakistan, work towards a just solution to this dispute.
Published in Dawn, September 30th, 2026
